@@41553713 <p> Prime Minister Boris Johnson has based most of his campaign around Brexit ( Photo : Chris J Ratcliffe/Getty ) <h> Brexit process/timing <h> Conservatives <p> Leave the EU on 31 January with an 11-month transition period during which nothing will change . Immediately start talks on a free-trade agreement with the EU . Do not extend the transition under any circumstances , even if talks over a comprehensive trade deal with Europe break down . If necessary , leave the transition period without a trade agreement at the end of 2020 . <h> Labour <p> Immediately agree a further delay to the Article 50 process , pushing the default Brexit date past summer 2020 . Negotiate a new Withdrawal Agreement with the EU within three months , based on the original text agreed by Theresa May but with major changes to the attached political declaration . This would include a transition period of uncertain length . This Brexit deal would be put to a referendum against Remain . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Write to the president of the European Commission revoking the UK 's Article 50 notification within hours of a new government taking office . This would end the Brexit process altogether , with the UK staying in the EU indefinitely on the same terms as now . <h> Green Party <p> Quickly agree a delay to Article 50 to give time for a referendum on membership of the EU , which would be held as quickly as possible . <h> Brexit Party <p> Either leave without a deal on 31 January , or negotiate a delay of a few months in order to agree a standstill under the terms of " Gatt XXIV " - this would see the UK and EU both agree to continue trading on the same terms as now while they hold talks on a comprehensive free-trade agreement laying out the permanent relationship . <h> Ukip <p> Leave the EU without any form of Withdrawal Agreement as soon as possible - which would almost certainly mean 31 January . Deal with the EU on World Trade Organisation terms while discussing a free-trade deal . <h> SNP <p> The party is totally opposed to Brexit given that Scots votes by 62 per cent to Remain in 2016 , and its manifesto says voting SNP could provide an " escape from Brexit " through independence . It adds that there is " no way " that the process of exiting the EU will be completed in the next few months and will instead go on " for years " as trade negotiations commence . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Delay Article 50 immediately to hold a second referendum on Brexit in the first few months of 2019 . Work with other pro-Remain parties to achieve this . <h> Summary : <p> The quickest way to resolve the Brexit impasse is to revoke Article 50 immediately as the Lib Dems suggest . Next would be leaving on 31 January as currently scheduled , while holding a second referendum would extend the process by several months . No party admits the truth : that whether we Leave or Remain , and whoever is in power , the Brexit row will rumble on for years . <h> Trade relationship with EU <h> Conservatives <p> A " zero tariff , zero quota " arrangement which would mean goods travelling between the UK and Europe with no taxes , in unlimited quantities . The UK would stay outside the single market and customs union , although Northern Ireland would keep the rules of both . That would mean checks on imports and exports to ensure that British manufacturers are not breaching European standards . <h> Labour <p> Enter into a customs union with the EU which would also feature " close alignment with the single market " . The intention would be to deliver the " exact same benefits " of the status quo so that all British businesses can continue to trade with Europe on identical terms as now and there is no change to arrangements on the Irish border . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Continue trading with the EU on the same terms as now . Take a leading role within the EU to deepen economic ties between member states . If Brexit does happen , the party will push for the closest possible economic relationship including membership of the customs union and single market . <h> Green Party <p> The Greens support greater European integration and radical reform of EU institutions , such as moving legislative power to the European Parliament and abolishing the EU seat in Strasbourg . They propose a Europe-wide minimum wage , an EU carbon tariff and " fiscal transfers " within the eurozone so that richer countries subsidise the budgets of poorer ones . <h> Brexit Party <p> A " Canada-style " trade deal with no tariffs on goods between Britain and Europe , but no commitment for the two sides to align their customs or regulatory regimes . This could mean checks on all goods going between the UK and EU , including those crossing the Irish border . <h> Ukip <p> Strike a loose trade arrangement with the EU , where both sides agree not to impose tariffs on each other but otherwise keep " regulatory independence " . This would create obstacles on the trade of goods , compared to the status quo . If the EU refuses , trade on WTO terms indefinitely . <h> SNP <p> If stopping Brexit proves impossible , the party will fight to protect Scotland 's place in the single market and customs union -- before ultimately seeking to rejoin the EU as an independent country . Its manifesto says its MPs will also work to prevent Scotland 's interests being used as " bargaining chips " in future negotiations with the EU or in any future trade agreement . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> If unsuccessful in keeping the UK within the EU , Plaid will push for Britain to stay in the single market and customs union - arguing they " are both essential for our home-grown employers and for attracting inward investment and job creation " . The party acknowledges this would be worse than EU membership because the UK would not have a say in setting the rules . <h> Summary : <p> The three pro-Leave parties all want some form of loose free-trade arrangement , although the Tories caveat that by creating a special status for Northern Ireland . If the pro-Remain parties fail to reverse Brexit they will all push for the closest trade relationship possible . Labour will offer a choice between soft Brexit and Remain . <h> Trade with rest of world <h> Conservatives <p> The Conservative manifesto pledges to strike free-trade agreements with the USA , Australia , New Zealand and Canada within three years . They also want to get trade deals with China and India in the longer term as well as other fast-growing countries in poorer parts of the world . The party says food standards and the NHS will not be up for negotiation in any trade talks . <h> Labour <p> Labour wants the new UK-EU customs union to be different from the existing customs union , so that Britain would have an independent say in any future trade deals between Europe and the rest of the world . The party would seek to block a trade agreement with the US if it included access to the UK 's health market for American firms . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Support the expansion of international trade in the face of opposition from nationalist leaders in other countries . Work with international agencies to ensure that global trade deals do not " worsen inequalities or undermine human rights " , and use the trading system to reduce corruption in poor countries . <h> Green Party <p> All trade deals must be environmentally friendly and protect employment rights . Carry out trade negotiations in public , with all documents published along with detailed assessments of their impact . Abolish " investor-state dispute settlement mechanisms " which allow companies to sue the government if they feel they are being unfairly excluded from markets . <h> Brexit Party <p> Strike free-trade agreements with as many countries as possible in order to make the most of the economic opportunities presented by Brexit . <h> Ukip <p> Halve all existing tariffs unilaterally and immediately . Set up a Commonwealth Free Trade Agreement to give preferential terms to other members of the Commonwealth . Strike trade deals with other countries , as long as they do not harm any British industry . Abolish investor-state dispute settlement mechanisms which Ukip calls " corporate courts " . <h> SNP <p> The party says a future trade deal with the United States could risk opening up the NHS to American multinational firms , as well as seeing the arrival of chlorinated chicken and hormone injected beef . Its manifesto also says its MPs will oppose any trade talks with Donald Trump until the US drops its new tariffs on Scotch whisky , introduced in October . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Do not prioritise a trade deal with the US . Ensure that any new trade agreements protect Welsh agriculture rather than immediately slashing tariffs . Give the Welsh assembly , as well as other devolved institutions , a formal say over whether or not to ratify future trade deals . <h> Summary : <p> In theory every party is in favour of expanding trade deals with other countries , but only the Conservatives hold the idea up as a top priority . The anti-Brexit parties would push to give Britain as much influence as possible over the EU 's trade policy , particularly in the event of fresh US-Europe trade talks . <h> Following EU standards <h> Conservatives <p> The political declaration attached to the Withdrawal Agreement guarantees a " level playing field " which means that UK standards could not fall below EU ones , but this is not legally binding . The Conservatives have promised to give Parliament a say on whether or not to approve any future move to reduce workers ' rights below those in Europe . They would relax rules on using state aid to invest in industry . <h> Labour <p> Dynamic alignment on rights for workers and consumers , as well as environmental protections , meaning that every time Brussels changes the law in any of these areas the UK would automatically do the same . Legally binding protection for level playing field provisions which would block any change to regulatory standards . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> The Liberal Democrats would oppose any trade deals which involved Britain lowering its regulatory standards on the ground that this would make it harder to do business with Europe . If they succeeded in keeping the UK in the EU they would urge other member states not to compromise existing standards on the environment and animal rights in any future trade deals . <h> Green Party <p> The Greens would keep existing EU regulations and work with other countries to expand them by banning factory farming , outlawing hunting for sport , ending the export of live animals and changing the Common Agricultural Policy and Common Fisheries Policy . <h> Brexit Party <p> The Brexit Party would abandon all European standards and make no commitment to a level playing field . This would allow the UK government to use public money to rescue troubled industries including the railways and steel manufacturers . There would be no future link between the EU 's regulatory standards and those which apply in Britain . <h> Ukip <p> Ukip promises to " reduce regulation to an appropriate level " by abolishing the laws businesses must follow due to our membership of the EU . But it would maintain existing laws on workers ' rights . <h> SNP <p> Pending Scottish independence , its MPs will press for the devolution of employment law so Holyrood can protect workers ' rights which it fears will be diluted after Brexit.The party 's MPs will also campaign for the UK to remain aligned with EU environmental regulations even if Brexit takes place , including sticking to future emissions standards . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Plaid has promised to threaten any moves which might " weaken the standards and rules on food safety and medicines " . If Brexit does take place the party favours keeping all existing European rules and regulations indefinitely . <h> Summary : <p> Apart from the Brexit Party and Ukip , all the parties want to keep or even increase the current level of regulation in areas such as the environment and workers ' rights . But leaving the EU would open the door to changing this in future , whatever manifesto promises are made . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Promised an extra ? 10.5bn for schools in England by 2024-25 compared to 2019-20 . Schools will be required to have " inclusive " and gender-neutral uniform policies . <h> Green Party <p> Promised to increase funding on schools by at least ? 4 billion per year . Other parties blame it for driving away teachers . <h> Universities <h> Conservatives <p> The Conservative manifesto is tight lipped on the future of university funding . Reskilling adults is likely to become more important . <p> The NHS has been a crucial topic in this election campaign ( Photo : Getty Images ) <h> NHS spending <h> Conservatives <p> Pledged to invest an extra ? 34bn cash in the NHS by 2023-24 compared to 2018-19 budgets , amounting to a 3.1 per cent increase in spending per annum . Will create Innovative Medicines Fund to combat cancer and autoimmune disease and introduce a national child vaccination reminder system . Suggests new planning laws to ensure greater emphasis on green spaces and cycle ways . <h> Summary : <p> Each party has pledged more funding for the NHS with Labour far outstripping its rivals . But whereas most parties aim to use the tax system to fund them , the Tories do not . <h> Staffing <h> Conservatives <p> The Tories have also pledged 50,000 more nurses , although this has been disputed as it is made up of retaining 19,000 nurses . Says it will use additional funding to bring down operating waiting times , improve A&amp;E performance and increase cancer survival rates . <h> Labour <p> The party is strangely less ambitious with its staffing pledges , promising to deliver 24,000 extras nurses and midwives . Party adds it will encourage the recruitment of hospital doctors and GPs by waiving repayment of tuition fees while they work in the NHS , and we will reintroduce student bursaries for nursing and midwifery students . <h> SNP <p> SNP ministers at Holyrood have promised to invest ? 250m in primary care during the current parliament and are aiming to recruit 800 extra family doctors over the next decade . But figures published this week show the GP headcount has increased by only 55 on last year , with the public spending watchdog warning that meeting the target will be very tough . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Pledges to recruit an additional 1,000 doctors , 5,000 nurses and 500 dentists for the Welsh NHS . Will free up ? 90m by cracking down on use of agency staff in the health service . <h> Summary : <p> The recruitment and retention of NHS staff is acutely understood by all parties given the pressures the health system is under . While the Conservatives have come under fire for their arithmetic on additional nurses , they are among the most ambitious in this area . <h> Mental health <h> Conservatives <p> Promises to treat mental health with the " same urgency " as physical health , and will legislate to ensure patients suffering from mental health conditions , such as anxiety and depression , have greater control over treatment . <h> Labour <p> Labour will pump an extra ? 1.6bn a year to ensure new mental health standards are " enshrined " in the NHS . A further ? 2bn will be spent modernising hospital facilities to accommodate mental health patients . It will also spend ? 845m on a new Healthy Young Minds programme to " more than double " spending on children and adolescent mental health services . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> The Lib Dems will ringfence funding from its penny increase on income tax to ensure extra investment on mental health . It will also introduce a maximum waiting time limit for mental health problems , and increase access to a broader range of " clinically effective " talking therapies . It has also pledged to give free prescriptions on the NHS to people suffering chronic mental health problems . <h> Green Party <p> Says it will focus funding on improving mental health care to put it on an equal footing to physical health . Promises " tailored and specific " provision for the particular needs of Lesbian , Gay , Bisexual , Trans , Intersex , Queer and Asexual ( LGBTIQA+ ) and the black and minority ethnic communities . <h> Brexit Party <p> The party states it wants the NHS to be a " beacon of excellent care " , but its " contract " does not mention mental health provision . <h> Ukip <h> SNP <p> A total of ? 250m has been pledged to support mental health services in Scotland over the next five years , including ? 60m for schools to improve counselling services and train staff . However , statistics published this week show that waiting time targets for young people are being missed in more than a third of cases , with more than 600 waiting for more than a year . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Pledges to increase mental health expenditure by 5 per cent every year for the next 10 years . Will also establish a 24/7 Mental Health Crisis Service for those in acute distress . <h> Social care <h> Conservatives <p> Despite claiming in August the Tories had a plan for social care ready to go , Boris Johnson has said he will build a " cross-party consensus " to develop a plan to solve the social care crisis . The party announced in the autumn an additional ? 1bn to prop up the social care system from April . It has also insisted nobody needing care should be forced to sell their home to pay for it . <h> Labour <p> Will build a " comprehensive " National Care Service for England . Will offer free personal care to all , starting with investing cash to ensure older people have immediate care needs met . Labour will also introduce a lifetime cap on personal contributions to care costs and ensure no one faces " catastrophic " care costs of more than ? 100,000 . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Perhaps the least ambitious part of the party 's health manifesto , it concentrates on rationalising the current care system involving local authorities more . It pledges to create a new care workers ' professional body to improve training and pay . It also states its wants to offer more choice at the end of life , and move towards free end-of-life social care . <h> Green Party <p> The Greens will pump an additional ? 4.5bn a year to fund councils to provide free social care to people over 65 needing support in their own homes . Says it will explore provision of free social care at home to all who need it , regardless of age . <h> Brexit Party <p> The party says it wants to introduce a new nursing qualification in social care to address the staffing crisis hitting the sector , but makes no offers beyond that . <h> Ukip <p> Will bring the social care into the NHS budget . Party insists social care should not put a person 's home and savings " in jeopardy if they have paid tax and national insurance all of their life " . Will increase social care funding in England by ? 5bn in the short term . <h> SNP <p> Personal care is already free in Scotland , with the SNP also promising to scrap fees charged for a raft of services provided by local councils in people 's own homes if it is re-elected in 2021 . However , the nation 's ageing population is steadily increasing the pressure on the system , with elderly people facing longer waits while their claims are assessed and processed . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Promises to provide free social care at the point of need , delivered by a new National Health and Social Care Service at a cost to the Welsh Government of an extra ? 300 million a year . <h> Summary : <p> Arguably the policy area that was Theresa May 's undoing in 2017 , and the scars are still felt by the Tories . The party 's manifesto ducks the issue this time around . Labour and the Greens promise an expensive free care for all . <p> What is each party promising to do with the economy ? ( Photo : Getty ) <h> Austerity <h> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson promises an end to the years of austerity under David Cameron and Theresa May . Before the election the Tories were already committed to raising spending on English schools by ? 7.1bn by 2023 , on the NHS by ? 34bn by 2024 and recruiting 20,000 extra police officers . Their manifesto added new promises of ? 2.9bn including a nurse recruitment drive and a blitz on potholes . <h> Labour <p> Pledges the " largest-scale investment in modern times " , as well as another ? 10.5bn for schools , to scrap tuition fees , inject an extra ? 26bn a year into the NHS , bring in a Real Living Wage of at least ? 10 per hour for all workers . In total its manifesto envisages around ? 80bn a year more spending as Labour argues sustained investment will produce economic growth . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Committed to another ? 33bn a year of spending , with the biggest focus on providing free childcare for English two , three and four year olds by 2024 at a cost of ? 13bn . This is more than four times more than the current provision . A further ? 7bn would be allocated to health and social care . An extra ? 10.6bn more would be spent on hiring 20,000 more teachers and cutting class sizes . <h> Green Party <p> Would bring austerity to a juddering halt , spending more than ? 1tn during the five-year Parliament . It will spend ? 100bn a year to cut carbon emissions by the hugely ambitious target of 2030 . Would spend ? 6bn a year more on the NHS , ? 4.5bn on social care and fund a universal basic income at a cost of ? 89bn a year . <h> Brexit Party <p> Unsurprisingly , all of the Brexit Party 's proposals for the economy and its spending plans are predicated on the UK leaving the EU in a " clean-break " departure . A " Brexit dividend " will be raised worth ? 200bn by scrapping HS2 , " keeping " ? 13bn annual contribution to the EU , clawing back ? 7bn from the European Investment Bank and cutting the foreign aid budget by half , which it says is worth ? 40bn over a five-year term . It is disputed whether these measures would raise the money it claims . <h> Ukip <p> Says it will be able to raise ? 70bn a year by virtue of leaving the European Union , cancelling major infrastructure projects , scrapping all foreign aid and abolishing around half of all government quangos . Pledges to invest in public services , such as schools , NHS and social care . <h> SNP <p> The party 's MPs will demand an end to austerity from the Westminster government and instead press for greater investment in public services and the economy , so Scotland can feel the benefits . Its manifesto argues austerity has caused " untold damage " to communities around the UK and pledges to oppose any Government does n't start to " replace the funds lost over the last 10 years " . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Believes the UK economy is heavily skewed towards the south east of England and London . As such , it calls for an end of the " outdated " Barnet Formula that calculates the nation 's finances and demands it is replaced by an Office for Fair Funding to deliver increased funding for Wales . <h> Summary : <p> Each of the parties promise to end austerity . While the Tories ' manifesto is relatively unambitious compared with its rivals , it still promises increases in public spending . Austerity will be well and truly consigned to history should the likes of Labour or Lib Dems come close to power with spending on frontline service set to soar . <h> Capital investment <h> Conservatives <p> Pledging to oversee an " infrastructure revolution for this country " , including heavy investment in railways , ? 29bn for road-building projects and spending ? 5bn towards ensuring every address in the UK has access to full-fibre broadband . Some rail lines closed during the Beeching cuts of the 1960s would be reopened . A ? 350m Cycling Infrastructure Fund would be established . <h> Labour <p> At the heart of Labour 's plans for revitalising the economy is a ? 400bn " national transformation fund " which would invest in infrastructure , renewable energy , house insulation , railways , electric cars and low-carbon technology . It promises a massive building programme of social housing and that full-fibre broadband would be available everywhere in the UK by 2030 . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Would pump ? 130bn into the national infrastructure . Would extend and upgrade railways and stations , invest in " cutting-edge energy technologies " , including tidal and wave power . Pledge to build at least 100,000 homes for social rent each year and ensure that total annual housebuilding increases to 300,000 . <h> Green Party <p> Will fund a vast capital investment programme worth ? 95bn , including building more zero carbon homes , while " retro-fitting " existing houses with insulation and other energy-saving measures at a cost of ? 24bn . It will scrap HS2 and spend ? 2.5bn a year on cycle infrastructure . <h> Brexit Party <p> Promises to invest at least ? 50bn in local road and rail schemes in what it describes as " development-starved " areas . Says it will partner with service providers to offer free " base-level " domestic broadband in deprived areas but puts not cost to it . Will also spend ? 2.5bn to regenerate the country 's fishing and coastal communities . <h> Ukip <p> Unlike most other parties , Ukip does not have an extensive programme for capital investment , but instead pledges to scrap major infrastructure projects , such as HS2 and the expansion of Heathrow . It does promise to spend money on expanding the rail network be re-opening lines cut in the 1960s . <h> SNP <p> The amount Scotland receives in its block grant from Westminster is determined each year and partly depends on spending decisions made by the UK Government in other areas . While the Tories have pledged a ? 3.1bn " windfall " for Scotland if its wins the election , the SNP has ruled out a deal with the party -- but it could work with Labour which has promised ? 100bn . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Has called for at least an extra ? 1.5bn a year to be spent on capital investment and allocated on a " needs basis " . The money would come from the UK government raising an ? 20bn a year over the next 10 years through borrowing . <h> Summary : <p> One area of the economy that is likely to see the most significant increase in spending is capital investment . Even the Conservatives are pledging to set new fiscal rules to spend ? 100bn on infrastructure projects . Labour dwarves it with a ? 400bn plan . <h> Personal taxes and VAT <h> Conservatives <p> Committed to a " triple tax lock " , guaranteeing that they will not raise the rates of the three biggest taxes - national insurance ( NI ) , income tax and VAT . They have indicated that they increase the NI threshold to ? 9,500 next year , with an " ultimate ambition " to lift it to ? 12,500 but no further details of the timescale . <h> Labour <p> Planned spending would be paid for by introducing a 45 per cent income tax rate on earnings over ? 80,000 and a 50 per cent rate on those with salaries of over ? 125,000 . Labour says only the top five per cent of earners would pay more under its " fairer tax " regime . National insurance rates would be frozen and Labour guarantees that VAT rates will not rise . Capital gains and dividend tax rates would be brought in line with new income tax rates . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Would raise all income rates by a penny in the pound in England , Wales and Northern Ireland , ring-fencing the ? 7bn extra cash for spending on the NHS and social care . The marriage tax allowance would be scrapped . The separate capital gains tax-free allowance would also be abolished and capital gains and salaries would instead be taxed through a single allowance . <h> Green Party <p> Plans to merge a variety of personal taxes , including employees ' national insurance , capital gains , inheritance and income tax into a single " consolidated income tax " . It says this will bring in an extra ? 20bn a year . Says it will replace the income tax threshold with Universal Basic Income , which will give ? 89 to every adult of ? 178 to families and pensioners a week . <h> Brexit Party <p> Makes no mention of income tax or National Insurance Contributions but pledges to abolish inheritance tax , which it describes as a " hated grief tax " that brings in 1 per cent of total tax revenue . <h> Ukip <p> Will raise the personal income tax allowance from ? 12,500 to ? 15,000 over the next Parliamentary term . Aims to restructure income tax into two bands of 20 per cent and 40 per cent with higher thresholds and will abolish inheritance tax ( currently ? 5.2bn per annum ) . It will also abolish stamp duty for UK citizens ' primary residences , but keep it for foreign purchases . <h> SNP <p> Scotland now sets its own rates and bands of income tax , but at Westminster the party says it will oppose tax cuts for the wealthiest and instead support a crackdown on tax avoidance and evasion . Its manifesto says its MPs will press the UK Government to freeze people 's National Insurance ( NI ) contributions and VAT rates , as well as calling for the devolution of NI to Scotland . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Would restrict income tax relief on pension contributions to the standard rate of 20 per cent , raising an estimated ? 11.5bn a year . Promises to raise employee national insurance contributions for higher and additional rate taxpayers from 2 per cent to 4 per cent pulling in around ? 2bn per annum . <h> Summary : <p> One of the areas where nearly all the parties are playing fast and loose with the truth . Most parties have pledged extra investment in public services , while suggesting tax rises will hit only the wealthiest or in the Tories ' case no one at all . But more spending must mean higher taxes or additional borrowing . <h> Business taxes <h> Conservatives <p> Government plans to cut corporation tax next year from 19 to 17 per cent would be scrapped to free up ? 6bn a year for public services . Business rates would be reduced with early cuts for pubs , music venues and small cinemas . A digital services tax would aim to ensure that major multinational companies pay " their fair share of tax " . <h> Labour <p> Corporate taxes would increase from 19 per cent to 21 per cent next April and to 26 per cent by 2023 . For small firms the rate would remain at 19 per cent until 2023 when it would become 23 per cent . A financial transactions tax would be brought in , along with a new tax on multinational firms operating in the UK but based overseas . Oil and gas firms would face a one-off windfall levy with the cash raised used to retrain workers in the industry . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Corporation Tax would be raised from 19 to 20 per cent with a pledge to " keep the rate stable with a predictable future path " . The party would triple the proposed digital services tax to six per cent . The most frequent fliers would be hit by plans to reform air passenger duty in a move that would raise around ? 5bn . A crackdown on tax avoidance is projected to raise ? 5.7bn . <h> Green Party <p> Plans to increase corporation tax from 19 per cent to 24 per cent , will raise the Bank Asset Tax . It also proposes abolishing both council tax and business rates and replacing them with a single land value tax that will also take in stamp duty on land . It believes this will capture the " real value of land , and the increased value arising from improvements to it " . <h> Brexit Party <p> Perhaps its most comprehensive policy area , the party promises to exempt 1m small businesses from corporation tax . It means all those firms with pre-tax profit of less than ? 50,000 will pay no corporation tax . <h> Ukip <p> Will keep corporation tax at 19 per cent with a view to lowering it over time . Post-Brexit it will cut VAT rates to zero on goods such as domestic fuel , sanitary products , and repairs to commercial , residential buildings . Will review council tax , and reduce business rates for high street shops , restaurants and pubs to zero with plans to replace it with an online sales tax for any online business with an annual turnover of ? 500,000 . <h> SNP <p> The party 's MPs will back an increase in the National Insurance discount businesses receive from ? 3,000 per firm per year to ? 6,000 , which it says will help relieve uncertainty caused by Brexit . As part of a crackdown on tax avoidance , it also wants to see tougher measures to improve the transparency of tax paid by international companies and a " fit for purpose " tax for online retailers . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Promises to freeze corporation tax at its current rate of 19 per cent , in a move similar to the Tories . Plaid believes this will raise ? 5bn . Taken together the tax policies will raise an extra ? 20bn , it says . <h> Summary : <p> Arguably the area of the tax regime that will be doing the heaviest lifting for most parties . Labour has suggested a vast proportion of its promises will be delivered by raising corporation tax . The Tories even abandoned their long held commitment to cut corporation tax to fund its plans . Business rates are also in line to tumble , whoever comes into power . <h> Pensions <h> Conservatives <p> The pensions triple lock , the winter fuel payment , the older person 's bus pass and other pensioner benefits would be retained , but the Tories reiterate that it is up to the BBC to fund free television licences for over-75s . Mr Johnson has said he can not promise to " magic up " money to compensate " Waspi women " hit by the change in the state pension age . <h> Labour <p> The ' triple lock ' on pension rises would be retained and Labour would guarantee the Winter Fuel Payment , free TV licences and free bus passes as universal benefits . Plans to raise the state pension age would be abandoned to leave it at 66 . Around 3.7m ' Waspi women ' , who claim they were not properly alerted to a rise in the pension age would be compensated at a total cost of ? 58bn . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Would keep the pension ' triple lock ' for the duration of the next parliament and would retain pensioner benefits such as winter fuel payments and free bus passes.The Lib Dems are committed to paying compensation to ' Waspi ' women who lost out when the state pension age went out . They say the parliamentary ombudsman would rule on the levels of compensation . <h> Green Party <p> Commits to giving all pensioners ? 178 a week - ? 10 higher than the current highest possible pension payment . Says it will look to address the " injustice " affected by hundreds of thousands of Waspi women . <h> Brexit Party <p> Promises to launch a " review " of the position of Waspi women , which it says were " unexpectedly short-changed " by the rise in the state pension age . <h> Ukip <p> Describes the state pension as a " Ponzi scheme " . Will maintain the triple lock on the state pension and review the national insurance system to ensure it delivers higher , more sustainable pensions . Will " deliver a solution " to Waspi women . <h> SNP <p> With pensions reserved to Westminster , the party will continue to support the " triple lock " , ensuring they continue to rise by inflation , earnings or 2.5 per cent -- whatever is highest . Its MPs will also oppose any increase to the state pension age , continue to support the WASPI campaign and argue for the reversal of the cut to Pension Credit . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Will compensate the women affected by the rise in state pension age , and promises to maintain the triple lock on state pensions . <h> Summary : <p> Pensioners can breathe easy in this election as , on the whole , they are the best looked after demographic in this election . Almost all parties pledge to keep the " triple lock " . Waspi women will be worst off under the Tories , and will be completely compensated by Labour in a major ? 26bn pledge . <h> Northern Powerhouse <h> Conservatives <p> There is a commitment to building Northern Powerhouse Rail ( previously known as High Speed 3 ) between Leeds and Manchester , and then " focus on Liverpool , Tees Valley , Hull , Sheffield and Newcastle " . The Tories would also press ahead with the Midland Rail Hub scheme , improving links between Birmingham , Leicester , Nottingham , Coventry , Derby , Hereford and Worcester . <h> Labour <p> Promises a ' radical decentralisation of power in Britain ' , including relocating part of the Treasury to the North of England and building regional offices of government . Committed to delivering Crossrail for the North , linking Liverpool and Hull , and improving connectivity across northern regions . The projects would boost the economy of the north , helping to create hundreds of thousands of jobs , the party says . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Promise to " kickstart a devolution revolution " with a ? 50bn regional balancing programme to spread investment across all parts of the UK . Say they would put significant resources into infrastructure projects in the Northern Powerhouse and the Midlands Engine regions and boost research and development outside the ' golden triangle ' of Oxford-Cambridge-London . <h> Green Party <p> Will scrap HS2 , which is championed by many northern leaders but commits to ushering in a new " golden era " of ril travel , opening up links between towns and cities in the north and the midlands . <h> Brexit Party <p> Makes no specific mention of the Northern Powerhouse , but Nigel Farage has come under fire from northern leaders over its promise to scrap HS2 . <h> Ukip <p> Plans to scrap HS2 but will create free ports to " turbo-charge " the north of England in areas such as Immingham and Grimsby , Hull Port , the Hull and Humber rivers , Tees and Hartlepool , Liverpool , the Tyne , and Manchester airport . <h> SNP <p> Nicola Sturgeon has previously spoken of her ambition for Scotland to become the UK 's " real Northern Powerhouse " and her party has criticised the UK economy 's reliance on London . It has also called for the HS2 rail link to be extended to Scotland , something that is promised by Labour in its manifesto , which could also be a bargaining point between the two parties . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Wants to scrap the " wasteful and environmentally damaging " HS2 project , and plough the money saved into transport infrastructure more " fairly " across the UK . <h> Summary : <p> Most parties pledge to devolve decision-making to the regions , particularly the north . For northern leaders , pushing on with HS2 is paramount to deliver the idea of the Northern Powerhouse . Fewer than half of the parties commit to delivering the rail project , however . The Tories do pledge to push on with HS3 or " Crossrail for the North " , while Labour commits to the entire scheme . <h> Borrowing and debt <h> Conservatives <p> Promise not borrow to fund day-to-day spending , but would " invest thoughtfully and responsibly in infrastructure " . The IFS think-tank estimates that Tory borrowing would be just over two per cent of GDP which is broadly in line with their aim of balancing the current budget . The party insists its spending plans are consistent with their commitment to controlling the UK 's debts . <h> Labour <p> Argues the UK needs to " borrow to invest in long-term productive projects that will both save our planet and stand our public sector in good stead financially for decades to come " . The IFS thinktank says this implies borrowing of around four per cent of GDP without taking the ' Waspi women ' pledge into account . Labour says it aims to balance the current budget . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Say they would take advantage of historically low interest rates to increase borrowing for investment . The IFS thinktank said the Lib Dem proposals implied lower borrowing levels than suggested by the Labour or Conservative manifestos . It said : " They would appear to be the only one of these three parties which would put debt on a decisively downward path . " <h> Green Party <p> Its plans will mean an eye-watering additional operational expenditure of ? 141.5bn a year , which it says will be paid for by a mix of tax reforms and savings measures . It will borrow ? 94.4bn for capital expenditure . It says it " appreciates these are large numbers " . <h> Brexit Party <p> Does not go into specifics about what would be its fiscal rules if in power , but its priorities suggest that additional investment will come from its Brexit dividend . <h> Ukip <p> Rules out additional borrowing and aims to balance the national budget by reducing the budget deficit to zero and thereafter paying off our national debt . <h> SNP <p> As well as the annual block grant from Westminster , SNP ministers can now borrow up to ? 450m per year up to a maximum total of ? 3bn -- but the party wants these limits to be increased . Its manifesto says having greater flexibility would allow the Scottish Government to " invest in infrastructure and grow our economy " more effectively . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Will increase borrowing for investment in capital infrastructure to the tune of around ? 200bn over 10 years . On day to day spending will raise revenue via higher taxes rather than additional borrowing . <h> Summary : <p> Most parties pledge to devolve decision-making to the regions , particularly the north . For northern leaders , pushing on with HS2 is paramount to deliver the idea of the Northern Powerhouse . Fewer than half of the parties commit to delivering the rail project , however . The Tories do pledge to push on with HS3 or " Crossrail for the North " , while Labour commits to the entire scheme . <p> Commuters wait for trains at Clapham Junction train station in London , Monday , Jan. 8 , 2018 . Thousands of commuters face a week of mayhem from Monday as Southern , Greater Anglia and South Western Railway staff plough ahead with planned strike action . ( AP Photo/Frank Augstein ) <h> Heathrow <h> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson has been a long-standing opponent of Heathrow expansion but as Prime Minister has softened his position . Parliament has backed in principle a third runway , but the Tories offer only luke-warm support : making clear it is a private sector project and that Heathrow must show it can meet obligations on air quality and noise and that there is a realistic business case . There will be no new public money . <h> Labour <p> No mention of Heathrow in its manifesto , but shadow chancellor John McDonnell , a staunch opponent of expansion , suggested last month that a Labour government might scrap the project on the grounds that it clashes with the party 's pledges to tackle climate change . Labour previously gave its MPs a free vote in the Commons on Heathrow , and its lack of inclusion in the manifesto leaves the door open . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> All expansion on major London airports including Heathrow , Gatwick or Stansted would be banned , as would any proposals for a new airport in the Thames Estuary . All domestic flights would have to meet new rules on emisisons , with aircraft obliged to meet a " zero carbon fuels blending requirement " . <h> Green Party <p> All airport expansion - including at Heathrow - would be banned across England and Wales , while a new carbon tax would be applied to aviation fuel on domestic flights . VAT exemption for domestic flights would be scrapped . All advertising for flights would be banned . People who take more than one return flight a year , including the 15 per cent of people who take 70 per cent of flights , would have to pay a Frequent Flyer Levy . <h> Brexit Party <p> No mention of Heathrow , airport expansion , flights or emissions in the party 's " contract with the people " . <h> Ukip <p> Third runway at Heathrow airport would be blocked on the grounds that it would " destroy many villages and listed buildings " and increase pollution in the local area . The party is not , however , opposed to any airport expansion : instead it would back a second runway at Gatwick airport and encourage investment in regional airports . <h> SNP <p> The party still officially supports the construction of a third runway at Heathrow , but in May Nicola Sturgeon indicated the policy may be reversed after she declared a climate emergency . The SNP manifesto points out that many of Scotland 's remote and rural communities rely on air travel , with trials of low and zero emission flights set to begin in the Highlands in 2021 . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> The party is opposed to a third runway at Heathrow on cost and environmental grounds and its MPs will vote in Parliament against any expansion . Plaid says although Heathrow claims that expansion would cost ? 14bn , the figure could be as high as ? 30bn . <h> Summary : <p> The issue of Heathrow expansion has slipped down the political agenda in recent years but is bound to come back when the airport tries to push ahead with the project . Tories and Labour have both tried to skirt the issue because of the views of senior figures with constituencies near to the airport . Unsurprisingly , the biggest opponents are the Greens and Lib Dems . <h> Railways including fares &amp; HS2 <h> Conservatives <p> Investment in Northern Powerhouse Rail and the Midlands Rail Hub . Many of the smaller Beeching lines axed in the 1960s would be restored . Contactless ticketing extended to 200 more stations in the South East . Metro mayors would be given control over local rail services . HS2 would be put on the back-burner , after the Oakervee review found costs could be as high as ? 81bn and the northern leg not delivered until 2040 . <h> Labour <p> Railways brought back under public ownership to make fares " simpler and more affordable " , reduce fragmentation and increase staffing levels . The new publicly owned rail company would coordinate mainline upgrades and oversee electrification on all lines . A new Crossrail for the North would be introduced and HS2 would be delivered in full up to Scotland as part of a wider network of high-speed railways . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> National rail network to be extended with smaller stations reopened . Trains converted to ultra low emissions by 2035 . Rail fares for commuters and season ticket holders frozen for a parliament . Support for HS2 , Northern Powerhouse Rail and Crossrail 2 but with greater controls on cost , accountability and potential damage to habitats and woodland . Open up franchise bidding process to public sector companies , local authorities and not-for-profit organisations . <h> Green Party <p> Extend rail network to remove bottlenecks , improve journey times and increase freight capacity and reopen closed stations . HS2 cancelled completely to fund rail improvements . All railway lines between cities electrified . Short-distance rail franchises handed to councils or groups of councils to give local people more power . All railways brought back into public ownership within 10 years . <h> Brexit Party <p> Scrap HS2 and use money to invest at least ? 50bn in local road and rail schemes in the regions who have been cut off from or not benefited from the growth of the capital . <h> Ukip <p> HS2 would be scrapped altogether on cost and environmental grounds . Use some of the money saved on investing in existing railways to improve capacity and journey times , including reopening some of the branch lines closed in the Beeching era . Door left open to part-public ownership of railways , including a new government-owned company to run failing franchises . <h> SNP <p> The party wants the work of Network Rail to be devolved to Scotland , so ministers can have greater control over how the system operates , and has argued for HS2 to be extended north of the border . Regulated fares are set to rise by 3.2 per cent in January in line with England and Wales , but off-peak fares will be held at 2.2 per cent . Ministers say any fare freeze would hit the public purse . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> HS2 project would be scrapped altogether as it is " wasteful and environmentally harmful " . Instead invest in public transport more fairly across all of the UK . All major rail lines would be electrified by 2030 . There would be a trans-Wales railway to connect Wales ' coastal communities . <h> Summary : <p> There is little support for HS2 across the political parties , with only Labour and the Lib Dems fully in favour . A common theme throughout the pledges is for passengers and local communities to be given better access and control over rail services - a clear reaction to recent problems of long-running delays and cancellations by the major train companies . <h> Housing <h> Conservatives <p> At least one millions new homes over the next Parliament . New long-term fixed rate mortgages for first-time buyers , and Help to Buy extended to 2023 . Ban on sale of new leasehold homes , with ground rents restricted to peppercorn . No fault evictions abolished . Rough sleeping abolished by the end of the next parliament , paid for by new stamp duty surcharge on non-UK resident buyers . <h> Labour <p> Department for Housing created , new ' use it or lose it ' taxes on developers on stalled housing developments , zero carbon standard for new homes , and 150,000 new social homes a year . Definition of " affordable " housing , currently set at 80 per cent of market rents , replaced with new definition linked to local incomes . Leasehold scrapped . Private rents capped in line with inflation , no fault evictions scrapped . Rough sleeping ended within five years . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Pledge to build 300,000 new homes per year , including 100,000 for social renting . New homes built to zero carbon standards . Control of Right to Buy devolved to local councils . New Rent to Own model for social housing , with tenants given increasing stake in property through rent and ownership after 30 years . Council power to increase council tax by up to 500 per cent on second homes . <h> Green Party <p> More than 100,000 new council homes created a year . Energy efficient heating upgrades for one million homes a year . New homes built to eco standards that use 90 per cent less energy . All new developments to have local infrastructure like shops , schools and public transport to cut down on car use . Solar panels and other renewable energy generators for 10 million homes by 2030 . <h> Brexit Party <p> Simplify planning system for brownfield sites and make it easier to vary size and type of units per development . Make it easier for councils to borrow from government to build council homes . <h> Ukip <p> " Controlled immigration " to reduce demand on housing supply . End Right to Buy , which has reduced supply of social housing , and Help to Buy , which has pushed up house prices . One million new homes on brownfield sites , paid for in part by government grants . Review of leasehold . Building of energy efficient , modular housing encouraged . Green Belt protected and new maximum housing density introduced . <h> SNP <p> With housing devolved to Scotland , ministers have set a target of delivering 50,000 affordable homes -- including 35,000 for social rent -- by the end of the current Parliament in 2021 . The target is backed by more than ? 3.3bn , described by ministers as the biggest investment in affordable housing since devolution , but it is unclear yet whether or not it will be met in time . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Creation of a new National Housing Company to borrow against rents to pay for new social housing in Wales . Target of 20,000 new homes over five years . All new-build housing to be energy efficient and equipped with solar panels . Give local communities a greater say over new local developments . <h> Summary : <p> There has been a shift towards support for more social homes across the political parties , and greater support for renters - with most parties pledging to axe no fault evictions . There 's also a big emphasis on energy efficiency for all new-builds . For all the pledges of hundreds of thousands of new homes a year , there is still a challenge over where they will be built . <h> Flood defences <h> Conservatives <p> The government has faced criticism over its response to flooding in the past year , so the Conservatives have stepped up their pledge on flood defences , promising ? 4bn in new funding to protect communities from flooding . <h> Labour <p> Extra ? 5.6bn in funding to improve flood defences , with areas at risk in north west England , Yorkshire and the East Midlands given priority . Fire services would be given power to coordinate emergency response to local floods , while planning guidance for new developments in flood risk areas would be reviewed by a Labour government . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Investment in restoration of peatlands , heathland , native woodlands and wetlands to protect against floods as well as absorb carbon . Redirect agricultural support payments to organisations that protect the countryside including preventing flooding . Create a ? 5bn fund for flood prevention and climate adaptation over the next parliament , including introduction of standards for flood resilience in new developments . <h> Green Party <p> Reshape natural environment to minimise flooding with tree planting , soil restoration and other mitigation measures . Change the planning system to prevent new building on floodplains . <h> Brexit Party <p> No specific policies on flood defences in the party 's contract , but they have called for more tree-planting , which can help minimise flooding . <h> Ukip <p> Re-establish local drainage supervisory boards run by communities to plan for future flooding crises . Allow farmers and landowners to carry out work on their land to prevent flooding without risk of penalties . <h> SNP <p> Scotland 's first ever national flood risk management plan was launched in 2016 after mass evacuations in Aberdeenshire , bringing together 14 separate local strategies.These include 42 flood protection schemes -- including maintenance of existing defences -- set to be put in place by 2021 at a total cost of ? 235m , helping to protect up to 10,000 properties . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Investment in tree-planting including increasing native woodlands which would help minimise flooding . Greater emphasis on flood defences in planning guidelines . <h> Summary : <p> Recent major flooding in 2019 in Derbyshire , Yorkshire and the Midlands has pushed the issue higher up the political agenda . Most of the parties are concentrating on natural environment responses to mitigate against the worst deluges , such as rewilding of land and large scale tree-planting . <h> Road-building <h> Conservatives <p> Road-building and improvements on major highways and local roads to be paid for out of ? 28.8bn investment fund , as part of a wider National Infrastructure Strategy . This would include filling in of potholes . Upgrading the A55 in north Wales and deliver the M4 relief road to improve links with England . <h> Labour <p> Less focus on roads than other forms of transport , but adoption of a Vision Zero approach to UK road safety , which aims to stop all deaths and serious injuries . Investment in neglected local roads , with a focus on pavements and cycle paths . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> No mention of road-building in the Lib Dems ' manifesto , which has a greater focus on making environmentally friendlier public transport more accessible and cheaper for commuters . <h> Green Party <p> Shifting entire transport and planning system away from car use to local public transport and cycling . Stop all new road-building programmes including the road tunnel at Stonehenge , and introduce 20mph default speed limits on neighbourhood streets and 40mph in non-residential areas . New housing developments to have good local infrastructure to deter car use . Use ? 1.5bn of Vehicle Excise Duty to maintain existing roads . <h> Brexit Party <p> There is no mention of road-building in the party 's contract . <h> Ukip <p> Scrap all road tolls , which the party says increase costs to businesses and the public . Ban of any future pay-as-you-go road pricing and stop use of the hard shoulder for " smart motorways " . The party 's manifesto rails against " excessive " signage and road furniture , speed cameras and speed bumps . <h> SNP <p> A major ? 3bn project to dual the A9 between Perth and Inverness started in 2015 and is due to finish in 2025 , with a similar scheme on the A96 from Inverness to Aberdeen due to end in 2030 . After a series of delays the Aberdeen Western Peripheral Route also opened in February after four years of building work , significantly reducing journey times for local residents . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Very little reference to road-building , with a greater emphasis on public transport and environmentally friendly ways of travel . The party would introduce a bicycle use reward scheme to encourage people to stop using cars and reduce congestion . <h> Summary : <p> Road-building is an area where the parties are at their most diverse in policy pledges - with clear support for public transport over car use from the Lib Dems , Greens and Plaid Cymru . <h> Electric cars <h> Conservatives <p> The Conservatives are planning to invest ? 1bn in a fast-charging network for electric cars and vehicles , and will consult " on the earliest date " the sale of new conventional petrol and diesel cars can be phased out . An additional ? 220m has been earmarked to help develop the UK 's first all-electric bus town , the location of which is still being decided , and new low-fare high-frequency ' Superbus ' networks . <h> Labour <p> Labour hopes to position the UK at the forefront of the development and manufacture of ultra-low emission vehicles , and has set its sights on ending the sales of new combustion engine-powered vehicles by 2030 . Charging infrastructure and electric community car clubs will also be allocated cash , and the transition of public-sector car fleets and public buses to zero-emissions vehicles will also be fast-tracked . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Under the Lib Dems , every new car and small van sold by 2030 will be electric . Jo Swinson 's party hopes to accelerate the adoption of electric vehicles ( EVs ) by overhauling how they 're taxed , with plans to slash VAT on EVs to 5 per cent . The rate of installing car charging points , including residential on-street chargers as well as ultra-fast service stops , will be increased . <h> Green Party <p> While even electric vehicles produce pollution , low-emission vehicles represent an improvement on the current situation , according to the Greens . The party will incentivise the replacement of diesel and petrol vans , lorries and coaches with electricity-powered equivalents , and will require all existing petrol and motorway service stations to offer charging points by 2025 . Sales of new petrol and diesel-fuelled vehicles will be halted by 2030 . <h> Brexit Party <p> No mention is made of electric cars in the Brexit Party 's " contract with the people " . <h> Ukip <p> While vowing its support for open , free-market competition between petrol , diesel and electric vehicles , a Ukip government would end subsidies and vehicle tax exemptions for electric cars . Off-street parking and charging point provision in new housing and industrial developments would be encouraged through the local planning process , and the party claims it would support free-market solutions to increase charging station installation across England . <h> SNP <p> The SNP-led Scottish Government has committed to phase out new petrol and diesel cars and vans by 2032 , eight years ahead of the UK , and wants Westminster to follow suit . More immediately , in September ministers announced a ? 17m fund to help Scots buy less polluting ultra-low emission vehicles ( ULEVs ) by taking advantage of attractive loans . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Eight of the counties with the lowest number of public electric car charging points per person across Britain are found in Wales , leaving the country in danger of being left behind in the oncoming electric car revolution , Plaid Cymru has cautioned . The party has pledged its support to make the switch to an electric transport system by 2030 , and intends to work towards a wholly electric fleet of public sector vehicles . <h> Summary : <p> Lowering the current government 's target for ending the sale of new petrol and diesel cars and vehicles from 2040 to 2030 is a common goal shared by many of the parties , and the majority back the installation of more charging points across the UK in a bid to prepare for the impending electrical car revolution . The endorsement of electric car fleets for community use is another recurring theme . <h> Broadband <h> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson 's party has pledged to bring full-fibre and gigabit-capable broadband to every home and business across the UK by 2025 , alongside ? 5bn in public funding to connect premises which are not commercially viable in the hardest-to-reach 20 per cent of England . This will double the party 's previous commitment to supporting roll-out to the hardest 10 per cent , it announced in October . <h> Labour <p> One of Labour 's most highly-publicised electoral promises has been free full-fibre broadband for every home in the country by 2030 . Under the name British Broadband , the scheme would involve bringing Openreach ( BT 's home connectivity division ) under public ownership . Its operating costs will be covered by the taxation of multinationals , including tech giants , and jobs for all existing broadband infrastructure and retail workers will be guaranteed . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> All new homes built from 2022 under a Liberal Democrat government will have access to ultra-fast broadband , while ensuring all existing households and businesses are able to connect to super-fast broadband . Small and medium-sized businesses will be prioritised in the roll-out of hyper-fast broadband , and special focus will be given to connecting rural areas which are likely to have poor overall connectivity . <h> Green Party <p> A commitment to rolling out high-speed broadband and better connecting rural communities through reliable broadband and mobile internet , " delivered through councils who understand local connection needs " are the Green Party 's two connectivity policies outlined in their manifesto . <h> Brexit Party <p> Nigel Farage 's Brexit Party pledges to partner with service providers to bring " free base level domestic broadband " to deprived regions , and to introduce free Wi-Fi access to all public transport . <h> Ukip <p> Instead of backing the installation of fibre broadband in every home , Ukip wants to build a network of well-connected business incubators , known as net centres , in digitally deprived areas . These will allow start-ups and small-to-medium businesses to take advantage of ultra-high-speed connectivity it says will be measured in gigabits rather than the slower megabits . <h> SNP <p> The Scottish Government is investing ? 600m with the aim of delivering superfast broadband to all of the nation 's homes and offices by the end of the current Parliament in 2021 . The programme has been hit by contractual delays and it now seems unlikely the target will be met , but ministers say it is still far more ambitious than any other plan across the UK . <h> Plaid Cymru <p> Creating a publicly-owned Welsh broadband infrastructure and guaranteeing access to full-fibre broadband to every home and business in Wales by 2025 are among Plaid Cymru 's proposed communications infrastructure projects . The Welsh government announced ? 10m in funding for projects concentrating on delivering super-fast broadband to poorly served communities in mostly rural areas of the country during a debate on digital connectivity last month . <h> Summary : <p> Providing households in areas with low levels of internet connectivity with improved access is a priority across all parties with the exception of Ukip , which advocates for giving businesses the means to access faster connections instead . Labour , the Lib Dems and the Brexit party have voiced their commitment to delivering home broadband for free , though the details on how such a project would be funded differ . <p> Where do the parties stand on protecting the environment ? ( Photo : Getty Images ) <h> Climate change and net zero <h> Conservatives <p> Pledges to lead the global fight against climate change after the government became , in June , the first major economy to promise to become carbon neutral , by 2050 - a pledge that was welcomed although many said it should be done sooner . Will use the UK 's position hosting the UN Climate Change Summit in Glasgow in 2020 to put pressure on other nations to match its ambition . But believes that the North Sea oil and gas industry has a long future ahead and plans to support the industry in the next Parliament . <h> Labour <p> Committed to put the UK on track to be carbon neutral within the 2030s - after initially considering a concrete target of 2030 - and go faster if credible pathways can be found . This is still more ambitious than the Conservative party target . Create a National Investment Bank to provide ? 250 billion of loans for enterprise , infrastructure and innovation over 10 years to finance the transition to a low-carbon economy . Promises to create at least one million unionised jobs as part of what it 's calling its Green New Deal . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Promises to deliver a ten-year emergency programme to cut greenhouse gas emissions substantially straightaway and to be entirely carbon neutral by 2045 at the latest - five years ahead of the Conservative pledge but 10 years behind Labour.Wants the UK to take a leading global role in tackling the climate emergency . Will insulate all 2.5 million of the country 's low-income homes by 2025 , supported by a new ? 6bn fund over five years . <h> Green Party <p> The party has the most ambitious target of making the UK carbon neutral - pledging to do so by 2030 . As you might expect the party has the most ambitious set of environmental policies . They do n't come cheap at an estimated cost of ? 100bn a year , a figure which has raised a few eyebrows and questions about where the money will come from - but which the party says would be money well spent - transforming the economy and its prospects . <h> Brexit Party <p> As a new party with a much narrower focus than most of its rivals , it is maybe not much of a surprise that the Brexit Party 's " contract " says less about climate change and the environment than any other party - although it does promise to announce an unspecified " global initiative " at the UN at some point.Whereas UKIP is openly dismissive of moves to tackle climate change , the Brexit party opts to skirt the issue altogether - not mentioning the term at all . <h> SNP <p> Scotland currently has the world 's toughest legally-binding emissions reductions targets , with SNP ministers committing to reach net zero emissions by 2045 , five years ahead of the UK target . The party 's manifesto says its MPs will press UK ministers to match the Scottish targets but also warns that if Westminster 's timetable slips , there will be a knock-on effect north of the border . <h> Biodiversity <h> Conservatives <p> Promises to invest in nature , with a ? 640 million new Nature for Climate fund to support natural systems to soak up emissions . This will build on the party 's support for creating a new forest - the Great Northumberland Forest in the north of England . In total , the party pledges to grow an additional 75,000 acres of trees a year- or about 30 million trees - by the end of the next Parliament , as well as restoring peatland . <h> Labour <p> Pledged to plant two billion new trees by 2040 - or 100 million a year - the most of any party . Will introduce a Climate and Environment Emergency Bill setting out in law robust , binding new standards for decarbonisation , nature recovery , environmental quality and habitats and species protection . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Will plant 60 million trees a year and introduce requirements for the greater use of sustainably harvested wood in construction . Will set legally binding targets for improving water , air , soil and biodiversity , supported by at least ? 18 billion over five years . Plans to establish a Department for Climate Change and Natural Resources . <h> Green Party <p> Promises to plant 700 million new trees and to make half of all farms grow trees by 2030 . To reduce pesticide and fungicide use by at least half by weight by 2022 , phase out all non-agricultural uses of pesticides , and immediately ban the most harmful substances . Maintain a moratorium on production and import of genetically modified ( GM ) foods , including food from animals fed on GM feed . <h> Brexit Party <p> It promises to plant an unspecified number of " millions " of trees . <h> SNP <p> Earlier this week the SNP pledged to plant 36m trees in Scotland by 2030 to slow climate change , support biodiversity and increase rural employment across the country.Its manifesto says it will also press UK ministers to create new woodland , working towards an overall target of 60m trees being planted every year in the UK by 2025 . <h> Energy <h> Conservatives <p> The UK 's offshore wind industry is already the biggest in the world and the party promises to more than quadruple its current capacity to 40GW by 2030 - by which point it will be providing about a third of the UK 's electricity . Advocates of renewable energy would also like to see it relaxing an effective ban on onshore windfarms by reintroducing subsidies , although it 's not made any commitment to do so . Having placed a moratorium on fracking in England ( it does n't happen elsewhere in the UK ) and has officially ruled out relaxing the ban . However , it appeared to leave the door open for change arguing that it would not support fracking " unless the science shows categorically that it can be done safely " . <h> Labour <p> Will introduce a windfall tax on oil companies , so that the companies which knowingly damaged the climate will help cover the costs . Pledges to deliver nearly 90 per cent of electricity and 50 per cent of heat from renewable and low-carbon sources by 2030 . Will build 7,000 new offshore wind turbines , 2,000 new onshore wind turbines , enough solar panels to cover 22,000 football pitches . Will permanently ban fracking and build new nuclear power where needed for energy security . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Pledges to end fossil fuel subsidies by 2025 , and provide ' Just Transition ' funding for areas and communities negatively affected by the transition to net zero greenhouse gas emissions . Accelerate the deployment of renewable power and build more connections to continental power supplies to guarantee security of supply . Most ambitiously , it aims to be producing at least 80 per cent of the country 's electricity supply from renewable sources by 2030 , about double what it is now - a target that won it praise among campaigners . <h> Green Party <p> Will remove subsidies to the oil and gas industries and apply a carbon tax on all fossil fuel imports and domestic extraction.Introduce support and incentives to accelerate wind energy development , with a target for wind to provide around 70 per cent of the UK 's electricity by 2030 . Ban fracking , and other unconventional forms of fossil fuel extraction.Phase out of the UK 's remaining coal plants and coal mines , ensuing a just transition for workers affected.Prohibit the construction of nuclear power stations . <h> Brexit Party <p> Post Brexit , the party promises to cut VAT rates to zero on domestic fuel - saving an average ? 65 per household . <h> SNP <p> At Westminster , SNP MPs will propose a Green Energy Deal with the aim of ensuring that renewable energy schemes get the long-term certainty needed to support investment . The party is also proposing a Net Zero Fund that would set aside an expected ? 8.5bn of tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas and channel it into green projects . SNP ministers have also set out a policy of " no support " for fracking in Scotland , although they stopped short of an outright legal ban . <h> Air Pollution <h> Conservatives <p> Will support clean transport to ensure clean air , as well as setting strict new laws on air quality . Promises to consult on the earliest date by which it can phase out the sale of new petrol and diesel vehicles - which is currently set at 2040 . Said its first budget will prioritise electric vehicle infrastructure including a national plug-in network and gigafactory . <h> Labour <p> Pledged to tackle air pollution in part through a transport programme focused on creating better , publicly accessible local transport systems . By improving public transport , it aims to help people to become less reliant on their cars , and to improve quality of life in our towns and cities . To this end , it will increase funding available for cycling and walking - although it does n't say by how much . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Promises that , by 2030 , every new car and small van sold is electric . Invest in public transport , buses , trams and railways to enable people to travel more easily while reducing their impact on the environment . Accelerate the transition to ultra-low-emission transport -- cars , buses and trains -- through taxation , subsidy and regulation.Dedicate 10 percent of the transport budget to walking and cycling . Introduce London-stye Ultra-Low Emission Zones to ten other towns and cities in England and ensure that all private hire vehicles and new buses licensed to operate in urban areas are ultra-low-emission or zero-emission vehicles by 2025 - providing ? 2 billion to support this transformation . <h> Green Party <p> End the sale of new petrol and diesel fuelled vehicles by 2030 . Create a network of electric vehicle charging points across the country . Require all existing petrol stations and motorway service stations to offer electric vehicle charging points by 2025 . Stop the building of new runways and all increased road capacity - a move it says will save thousands of acres of countryside every year and protect people from the harm of increased air pollution . <h> Brexit Party <p> There is no mention of air pollution in the Brexit Party 's ' Contract with the People ' . <h> SNP <p> The Transport Bill passed in October gives councils the powers to introduce low-emission zones , which levy daily fees on polluting vehicles entering certain parts of cities.Glasgow will be the first to introduce one by the end of 2022 , with similar plans in Edinburgh , Dundee and Aberdeen . Green groups have criticised the proposal as being too weak and too slow . <h> Greenhouse gas emissions <h> Conservatives <p> The party has pledged ? 800m to develop new technology to capture CO2 before it gets into the atmosphere , known as carbon capture and storage ( CCS ) - and ? 500m to help carbon-intensive industries reduce their footprints . But no policy to tackle aviation emissions , a major source of greenhouse gases . Will look to cut emissions - and reduce energy bills - by investing ? 9.2 billion in the energy efficiency of homes , schools and hospitals . <h> Labour <p> Labour tabled the motion which led to the UK Parliament declaring a climate and environmental emergency , which it did earlier this year , becoming the first parliament in the world to do so . While the Conservatives have committed to ending sales of new petrol and diesel vehicles by 2040 , Labour will aim for 2030 . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Would accelerate the rapid take-up of electric vehicles ( EVs ) by reforming vehicle taxation , cutting VAT on EVs to 5 per cent and speeding up the installation of charging points , including residential on-street points and ultra-fast chargers at service stations . Place a moratorium on the development of new runways in the UK , opposing any expansion of Heathrow , Gatwick or Stansted and any new airport in the Thames Estuary . Increase tax on international flights to focus on those who fly the most , while reducing costs for those who take one or two international return fights per year.Would ban fracking . <h> Green Party <p> Promise to spend ? 2.5 billion a year on new cycleways and footpaths , built using sustainable materials , such as woodchips and sawdust . Create a new ' golden age ' of train by opening new rail connections that remove bottlenecks , increase rail freight capacity , speed up journeys and increase the frequency of trains.Prepare for the rapid decommissioning of North Sea oil rigs and the phasing out of the UK 's remaining coal plants and coal . <h> Brexit Party <p> The party has said it will scrap controversial HS2 high-speed rail link - a move that could reduce greenhouse gas emissions as the path threatens areas of woodland . <h> SNP <p> As well as its net zero by 2045 pledge , the SNP ministers have pledged to phase out new petrol and diesel cars and vans in Scotland by 2032 , eight years of the UK Government 's target . The party says this will be delivered by electrifying the road network and doubling investment in " active travel " - such as improving walking and cycling routes -- to ? 80m per year . <h> Waste/recycling <h> Conservatives <p> After China stopped receiving large quantities of the UK 's waste , the spotlight has been put on the issue of where our waste goes - with much being sent to developing countries that are ill-equipped to deal with it . The party would ban waste exports to all non-OECD countries and will only send it to nations with adequate facilities to recycle them . Penalties for fly-tipping will be increased and those on community sentences will be made to clean up parks and streets . <h> Labour <p> Will work with local authorities to reduce food waste and " learn from the Labour government in Wales " , where recycling rates have increased sharply in recent years . It will also set up a National Food Commission to tackle hunger and cut down on waste . The party points out that a quarter of all food purchased is wasted every year , equivalent to over 20 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions , costing over ? 20 billion . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Introduce a legally binding recycling target of 70 per cent - compared to around 50 per cent now . Extend household food waste collection schemes to at least 90 per cent of homes by 2024 - also compared to about 50 per cent now . Introduce a National Food Strategy , including the use of public procurement policy , to promote the production and consumption of healthy , sustainable and affordable food and cut down on food waste . <h> Green Party <p> Require manufacturers and retailers to pay the full cost of recycling and disposing of the packaging they produce - something that the existing government is looking at on a smaller scale . Argues that a ' circular economy ' will underpin its proposed green industrial revolution , ' designing out ' waste and pollution and keeping products and materials in use . Recycling and repairing will be made easier , reducing the need to buy new , expensive products on a regular basis , it says . <h> Brexit Party <p> The part wants the UK to recycle its own waste and make it illegal for it to be exported across the world to be burnt , buried or dumped at sea . <h> SNP <p> Under plans announced in May , Scotland is set to become the first part of the UK to introduce a Deposit Return Scheme for drinks containers in an effort to boost recycling rates .
