Plastic and glass bottles or aluminium drinks cans sold in shops , pubs and restaurants will carry an extra 20p surcharge , which can be reclaimed by customers when they are returned empty . <h> Oceans/plastic <h> Conservatives <p> Will establish a new ? 500 million Blue Planet Fund to help protect oceans from plastic pollution , warming sea temperatures and overfishing.Will " continue to lead diplomatic efforts " to protect 30 per cent of the world 's oceans by 2030 . Introduce a levy to increase the proportion of recyclable plastics in packaging and a deposit return scheme for plastic and glass . Pledged ? 4 billion for new flood defences as rising sea levels threaten ever greater floods . <h> Labour <p> Will tackle the plastic pollution problem by making " producers responsible for the waste they create and for the full cost of recycling or disposal , encouraging more sustainable design and manufacturing . " It also pledges end the export of plastic waste to reduce our contribution to ocean pollution , but did n't put a timeline on this . <h> Liberal Democrats <p> Ban non-recyclable single use plastic within three years . Establish a ? 5 billion fund for flood prevention and climate adaptation over the course of the parliament to improve flood defences , and introduce high standards for flood resilience for buildings and infrastructure in flood risk areas . Set up a ' blue belt ' of marine protected areas covering at least 50 per cent of UK waters by 2030 , in partnership with UK overseas territories . There is no policy to address North Sea oil and gas . <h> Green Party <p> Ban the production of single-use plastics for use in packaging and invest in research and development into alternatives to plastic . <p> Extend the tax on plastic bags to cover plastic bottles , single-use plastics and microplastics , and extend plastic bottle deposit schemes.Open up more coastal waters for offshore wind and marine energy . <h> Brexit Party <p> Pledges to invest ? 2.5 billion in fishing and coastal communities , adding that Brexit would allow the UK to recover control of a 200 mile exclusive economic zone which would create the opportunity to regenerate coastal communities . <h> SNP <p> As well as the Deposit Return Scheme , which it is hoped will be up and running within two years , Scotland also banned the sale and manufacture of plastic-stemmed cotton buds in October . SNP ministers are also consulting on a proposal to create Europe 's largest marine protected area off the Western Isles , with the aim of protecting coral reefs and other marine life from interference . <p> A Universal Credit sign in the window of the Job Centre in Westminster ( Photo by Jack Taylor/Getty Images ) <h> Disability <h> Conservatives <p> The party will publish a new National Strategy for Disabled People before the end of next year . This will combine existing commitments to improve the benefits system with proposals to increase access to housing , education , jobs and transport . There is a pledge to reduce the disability employment gap . <p> Labour <p> Alongside changes to benefits , a new Department for Women and Equalities will oversee changes including a requirement that employers are better trained to accommodate disabled workers and a mandatory reporting on any disability pay-gap for companies with more than 250 employees . Disability leave will be paid and recorded separately from sick leave . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> An extra ? 6bn per annum will be invested in the social security system , including a pilot scheme rewarding employers for investing in their employees ' mental wellbeing . Cuts to the Employment Support Allowance will be reversed . More stations will be made accessible for wheelchairs . <p> Green Party <p> Alongside its plans to overhaul benefits , the party will introduce measures including a requirement for councils to draw up disability housing plans and increase the number of homes built to disabled mobility standards . There will be increased support for disabled people to enter politics and stand for office . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party 's proposed " contract " with the British people makes no specific mention of policy for the disabled . It proposes changes to the Universal Credit benefit ( see below ) . <p> UKIP <p> The party states that it is committed to protecting the rights of the disabled and supports their " inclusion in the workplace whenever that is possible " . It proposes an increase in public toilet provision with more disabled access . <h> SNP <p> A raft of disability benefits are in the process of being devolved to Scotland , including Personal Independence Payments and Disability Living Allowance , which are being rolled out in phases . The party 's manifesto says its MPs at Westminster have been " instrumental " in forcing UK ministers to rethink proposed cuts to disability benefits and promises to keep up the pressure . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party proposes a return to sheltered employment schemes for those with disabilities , which will serve as a " stepping stone " towards full employment . It also proposes an Autism Act for Wales , giving full protection under equalities law to those with the condition . Disabled people should not face the same benefits threats and sanctions that the able-bodied do in seeking employment . <p> Summary : <p> The parties pledges attempt to address problems with the benefits system and action to ensure the disabled have fair access to the jobs market . Disability rights groups argue that the disabled still face discrimination and a lack of concerted action . <h> Universal credit and minimum wage <h> Conservatives <p> The party is committed to continue the roll-out of the controversial six-in-one benefit and pledges to do more to ensure that it works " for the most vulnerable " as well as supporting the main carer in every family . The age limit for the National Living Wage will be lowered to 21 ( currently 25 ) and reach ? 10.39 per hour by 2024 . <p> Labour <p> Jeremy Corbyn has pledged to scrap Universal Credit and replace the Department for Work and Pensions with a new Department for Social Security . It promises an alternative benefits system that " treats people with dignity and respect " , including scrapping work capability assessments . It wants to introduce a minimum standard of living . The minimum wage will be increased to ? 10 per hour as a Real Living Wage for all employees aged 16 and over by 2020 . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Universal Credit will be reformed rather than scrapped . The maximum wait for first payments will reduced from five weeks to five days and the two-child limit will be abolished . The sanctions regime will be replaced with an " incentive-based scheme " . People on zero-hours contracts will receive a 20 per cent higher minimum wage to compensate for the uncertainty of fluctuating hours of work <p> Green Party <p> A Universal Basic Income ( UBI ) will replace Universal Credit by 2025 . This will provide a weekly payment of ? 89 for everybody - including the employed - and replace the current benefits system . Added income would be available for groups such as the disabled and single parents . Workers on zero-hours contracts would receive at least the minimum wage and the UBI will be worth at least up to 15 per cent than the minimum wage for those working 37.5 hours per week . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party states that Universal Credit " needs to be revisited " and it will undertake a 12-month review with reforms to follow within two years . Its election " contract " makes no mention of the minimum wage . <p> UKIP <p> The party states that Universal Credit is based on " good principles " including " ending incentives to stay unemployed " . But it says the benefit should not be implemented in a way that causes " unnecessary hardship " . It will seek to limit the use of zero-hours contracts to ensure " everyone can earn a living wage " . <h> SNP <p> The party says Universal Credit is causing " real hardship " and should be radically reformed by scrapping the two-child cap on child tax credits and the " appalling rape clause " . Powers over the minimum wage are reserved to Westminster , but the party 's manifesto calls for employment law to be devolved to Scotland so it can increase the living wage . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party pledges to take control of Universal Credit in Wales to reverse the effects of " a decade of austerity " . It opposes the use of zero-hours contracts and seeks a " real living wage " for those working in the public sector or for private companies servicing the public sector . <p> Summary : <p> With the predictable exception of the Conservatives , all parties are pledged to either scrapping or reforming Universal Credit . The Greens have arguably the most radical policy of introducing a guaranteed single income to replace existing benefits . <h> Flexible working , four-day week <h> Conservatives <p> The party will consult on making flexible working a " default " unless employers can put forward good reasons why it is not suitable . Employees will also have the right to demand a " predictable contract " . Party leader Boris Johnson has described Labour 's idea of a four-day week as a " crackpot plan " . <p> Labour <p> An entitlement to flexible working will mean every employee would have the right to choose the pattern of their working hours from their first day in a job . Employers would also be obliged to have a menopause policy , including flexible working , for all women . The party aims to introduce a 32-hour full-time working week within a decade , though this could vary by sector . Think-tanks have put the cost of the four-day week at between ? 3bn and ? 17bn . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Flexible working will be available to all employees from day one of employment unless employers can put forward a strong case why that should not apply . Agency workers will have the right to a fixed-hours contract after 12 months of employment . <p> Green Party <p> Under a " quality of life guarantee " , people will have a right to flexible hours , in particular those with young children to ensure those who wish to return to work can do so . The party will " support employers to explore four day working weeks " with the aim of increasing productivity and boosting the wellbeing of staff . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party states that leaving the European Union will free the UK from rules such as restrictions on state aid to create thousands of new jobs in strategic industries . It makes no specific pledges on flexible working or the length of the working week . <p> UKIP <p> The party states that " on leaving the EU , UKIP will protect workers ' rights " . It makes no specific pledges on flexible working or the length of the working week . <h> SNP <p> Strongly supports flexible working . The SNP-led Scottish Government has commissioned a feasibility study for a " Centre for Flexible Work " to design and test new approaches in this area . A motion calling for the party to examine the possibility of a four-day week was submitted to the party 's spring conference this year , but it did not make it onto the final agenda . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party says it supports the right of workers to seek flexible working arrangements , particularly women and those with young families . It has pointed out that a lower proportion of employers offer flexible working in Wales than in England and Scotland . <p> Summary : <p> Flexible working is a buzzword in many party manifestos , often presented as part of a package to reform the modern workplace . Only two parties have formally expressed a desire to shorten the working week . <h> Parental rights - childcare <h> Conservatives <p> The party will invest in " wraparound childcare " , meaning provision will be increased for after school and during holidays as part of a ? 1bn fund to create more " high-quality and affordable " childcare and ensure parents do not have to choose between family and their careers . <p> Labour <p> A package worth ? 4.5bn will be spent on opening 1,000 new early years Sure Start centres and extending the entitlement to 30 hours of free childcare to all children between two and four . The party says it wants to see the early years sector move towards a " qualified , graduate-led workforce " and improve the pay and skills of childcare workers . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> A total of 35 hours free childcare will be available to working families from the age of nine months as part of a ? 14.6bn " investment in the country 's future " . All children aged two to four will be eligible for 35 hours of funded childcare for 48 weeks a year , regardless of their parents ' working status . <p> Green Party <p> A total of 35 hours per week of free childcare for all children from the age of nine months . This will include workplace creches to allows parents greater flexibility with returning to work . The measure is part of an ? 86.2bn " green new deal " . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party pledges to invest in education and expanding parental choice . It makes no specific pledges on childcare or early years funding . <p> UKIP <p> The party is opposed to free universal childcare for three and four-year-olds , arguing the policy is poorly targeted and has led to distorted prices . It will scrap universal provision and instead target childcare subsidies towards the most disadvantaged families . Business rates on childcare centres will also be reduced to zero . <p> SNP <p> Pressure UK ministers to increase maternity leave to a year and set maternity pay at 100 per cent of average weekly earnings for the first 12 weeks , then 90 per cent for 40 weeks or ? 150 , whichever is lower . In Scotland , the Sure Start grant has been replaced with a new expanded payment giving eligible families ? 600 on the birth of their first child and ? 300 on the birth of any subsequent children . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party will offer universal free childcare for 40 hours per week across Wales . It will also introduce a new ? 35 per week payment for every child in low-income families to tackle child poverty . <p> Summary : <p> There is clear movement towards more state-funded childcare in the early years . Much of this is presented as part of a package to help young families and encourage a return to work . <h> Industrial relations <h> Conservatives <p> A single enforcement body will be created to " crackdown " on any employers abusing employment law , for example taking tips or refusing sick pay . There will be a requirement for a " minimal service " during transport strikes , though it is not explained how this would work . <p> Labour <p> The party will remove " unnecessary restrictions " on industrial action while also enforcing the right of trade unions to enter workplaces . Protections for trade union representatives will be increased and the law around union recognition will be simplified . The party has denied that it will allow the return of secondary picketing but stated it will uphold the right of people to withdraw their labour . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The ability of unions to represent workers " effectively in the modern economy " will be strengthened , including the introduction of a right to access workplaces . A new Worker Protection Enforcement Authority will be set up to safeguard those in " precarious work " . Employees in listed companies with more than 250 staff will have a right to request shares . <p> Green Party <p> The party pledges to " revive the role of deomcratic trade unions " and require employers to recognise any union that their staff have chosen to represent them . Major companies will have a requirement of at least 40 per cent female representation on their boards . <p> Brexit Party <p> Employers will be encouraged to invest in jobs and be involved in training and apprenticeships . Its proposed " contract " with voters does not make specific pledges on industrial relations . <p> UKIP <p> The party pledges to " protect workers ' rights " on leaving the European Union . It will reintroduce so-called " Whitley councils " or joint employer/employee negotiating bodies in the civil service . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party states that Brexit is a threat to workers ' rights and will protect or extend those rights with measures including a legal ban on pregnant women being made redundant or until six months after maternity leave . Employment Action Zones will also be established in areas of high joblessness with exemptions from National Insurance for employers . <p> SNP <p> Industrial action is n't specifically mentioned in its manifesto as the law in this area is reserved , but the party 's MPs will press for the devolution of employment law to allow the Scottish Parliament to protect workers ' rights . <p> Summary : <p> The Labour Party , partly funded by unions , puts forward a clear set of reforms to bolster the role of unions . Elsewhere there are pledges to do more to protect employees from unscrupulous employers . <h> Equality <h> Conservatives <p> The party makes several pledges , including an undertaking to " vigorously combat harassment and violence " against all religious groups and the LGBT community . It will set up a Constitution , Rights and Democracy Commission to examine what is the " proper balance " between the rights of the individual , national security and effective government . The party says it will fight health inequality and promote equality of opportunity in schools . <p> Labour <p> There will be a new Department for Women and Equalities with a Cabinet-level minister whose responsibilities will include ensuring all policies and laws are assessed for impact on equality and inequalities . In particular , the party says it will close the gender pay gap by 2030 and extend pay-gap reporting to include ethnic minorities . It will maintain funding to protect places of worship and consult on putting religious community protection groups on a statutory footing . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The party states that it will defend the Human Rights Act and resist any attempt to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights . All hate crimes will be automatically classed as aggravated offences . A gender " X " option will be introduced for passports and equality law will be extended to cover gender identity . LGBT+ status will be included as a question within the 2021 census . <p> Green Party <p> The gender pay gap will be closed with all medium and large companies required to conduct audits and then redress inequalities of pay . The law will be changed to make it easier to take action against employers on this issue . The parental opt-out for children learning about LGBT relationships will be ended . All political parties will be required to report the diversity of their candidates . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party has an over-arching pledge to change British politics " for good " while not itself seeking to form a government . It offers a new power to initiate referendums subject to a threshhold of five million signatures of registered voters . <p> UKIP <p> The party will repeal the Equality Act 2010 , which it says wrongly gives special rights and privileges to groups with " protected characeristics " and instead introduce a law for " general non-discrimination " . It will also disband the Equalities and Human Rights Commission , which its describes as indulging in " Cultural Marxist social engineering of society " . It also opposes any law to make gender a " self-declared condition " . <p> SNP <p> In Scotland , the voluntary Scottish Business Pledge scheme already encourages firms to pay workers the living wage , close the gender pay gap and never use exploitative zero-hours contracts . The party says its MPs will also back moves to increase worker representation on company boards and argue for greater representation of women and minority communities . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Support for the LGBT community will include a requirement for schools to keep a register of bullying based on sexuality and promotion of participation in sport . A reform of the Equality Act 2010 will introduce the concept of " gender identity " and remove the use of the terms " gender reassignment " and " transsexual " . <p> Summary <p> Parties across the political want to be seen to address equality issues and there is some new thinking on measures to bolster equality measures . Perhaps unsurprisingly , left-leaning parties place more emphasis on ensuring equality across society . <h> Pensioner benefits <h> Conservatives <p> The party will keep the triple lock on the state pension , meaning it will rise in line with whichever is highest of wages , prices or 2.5 per cent . The winter fuel payment , the pensioner bus pass and other benefit will be kept to " ensure that older people have the security and dignity they deserve " . The party believes free TV licences for the over-75s should be kept and paid for by the BBC . <p> Labour <p> The party guarantees that pensioner benefits will be protected , including the Winter Fuel Payment and free bus passes . It will also ensure the restoration of free television licences for the over-75s . The state pension age will remain at 66 and plans to raise it will be abandoned . Retirement ages in physically arduous jobs will be reviewed . The " triple lock " will be maintained on the state pension . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The triple lock will be retained on the state pension , meaning it will rise in line with whichever is highest of wages , prices or 2.5 per cent . The system of pension tax relief will be reformed . <p> Green Party <p> The party 's Universal Basic Income policy will replace the state pension and pensioner benefits will be maintained , such as free television licences . The UBI will stand at ? 178 per week for all pensioners , regardless of income or savings - this is ? 10 higher than the current highest state pension level . There will be a supplement for lone pensioners . Pensioners in need of home care in England will receive it for free <p> Brexit Party <p> The party states that providing a safety net is a " defining mark of a civilised society " but makes no specific pledges on pensioner benefits . It states it will review the position of so-called WASPI women born in the 1950s and short-changed by rises in the pension age . <p> UKIP <p> The party will maintain the state pension " triple lock " and pledges a review of the National Insurance system to investigate " higher and more sustainable pensions " . It suggests options include the creation of a Sovereign Wealth Fund to underpin the state pension using the proceeds of the UK 's natural gas reserves . <p> SNP <p> Will fight to reverse cuts to pension credit , which it says could leave older couples in Scotland around ? 7,000 per year worse off , and campaign to keep the BBC licence fee free for over-75s . Its manifesto points out that pension credit has one of the lowest take-ups of any benefit and calls for a national awareness campaign to ensure it is paid out to the maximum number of people . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Pensioner benefits will be maintained , along with the state pension " triple lock " . The free bus pass will therefore remain and the BBC will be required to reverse the cuts to the free television licence . The party will also support keeping public toilets open in town centres and other locations so older people can maintain their independence . <p> Summary : <p> Most parties are careful to emphasise the continuation of existing pensioner benefits and assurances about the level of the state pension . No votes are won by pledging to reduce safeguards for the elderly . <p> Britain and the world <h> Security <p> Conservatives <p> 20,000 more police officers on the streets with extra powers to stop and search and target known knife carriers , prevent more foreign national offenders entering the UK , expand role of police and crime commissioners and introduce a new national cyber crime force using new technologies . New law to protest emergency workers from assault , strengthen National Crime Agency , improve safety and security at public venues in wake of 2017 Manchester Arena terror attack and a new Victims ' Law to guarantee victims ' rights . <p> Labour <p> 2,000 more police officers than the Conservatives , extra resources to tackle wildlife crime , new law to protect emergency workers , work to eliminate institutional bias against black and ethnic minority communities , improve police training on domestic abuse and overhaul cyber security . On terrorism , ensure closer coordination between police and security services , and review the Prevent counter-radicalisation programme to safeguard those vulnerable to recruitment propaganda . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Adopt a " public health approach to serious violence " with ? 500m to restore youth services and ? 1bn for community policing , enough for two new police officers in every ward , with cooperation from teachers , health professionals and youth workers to stop young people falling into gangs . Introduce youth intervention specialists in all major trauma centres , more funding for the National Crime Agency , end disproportionate use of stop and search and more funding to tackle domestic abuse and support victims . <p> Green Party <p> Invest in youth services to deter young people from getting into gangs , more funding for community policing including more liaison and equality officers to work on improving relations with local communities . Make misogyny a hate crime and increase resources for police to deal with domestic violence . <p> Brexit Party <p> Withdrawal from the EU with a " clean-break Brexit " to control the UK 's own national security and borders . Increase police numbers and fund more visible policing with a focus on combating violent crime , robbery and burglary as a priority over enforcing restrictions on free speech . Target county lines drug dealers , gangs and the growth of knife crime . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Would phase in an increase in spending on foreign aid from 0.7 per cent to 1 per cent of our gross national income ( GNI ) , making us the third highest donor , by that measure , in the world by 2021 . Ensure that all UK aid is aimed at the poorest , and is locally designed , appropriate and subject to local scrutiny . Where feasible , aid will be given as grants , not loans . <h> Defence <p> Conservatives <p> Pledges to continue meeting Nato 's target of spending two per cent of GDP on defence and promises increases of at least 0.5 per cent above inflation every year . Would maintain the Trident nuclear missile system and build the new Type 31 frigates in shipyards such as Rosyth and a new generation of armoured vehicles . Would increase investment in cybersecurity . <p> Labour <p> Would maintain Britain 's commitment to Nato and spend at least two per cent of GDP on defence . Promising to use the UK 's commitment at the United Nations to " support peace and security worldwide " , would increase funding for UN peacekeeping operations to ? 100m . Armed forces pay would be boosted by scrapping the public sector pay cap . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Committed to spending two per cent of GDP on defence in line with Nato stipulations . Say they would maintain a " minimum nuclear deterrent " while pursuing multilateral nuclear disarmament and press ahead with the Dreadnought submarine programme . Pledge to address skills shortages by giving ? 10,000 " golden handshakes ' to graduates who become armed forces engineers . <p> Green Party <p> The Ministry of Defence would be replaced by a Ministry for Security and Peace and subsidies for arms manufacturers would be scrapped . <p> Brexit Party <p> The UK would spend an " absolute minimum " of two per cent of GDP on defence . By leaving the European Defence Union , the UK would have the right to stipulate defence contracts remain in the UK . Would invest in defence industry , creating thousands of jobs . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Is demanding a vote of approval in the Welsh Assembly before the UK is involved in foreign wars . Committed to providing " excellent " healthcare to veterans and " adequate " housing for former service personnel . <h> Prisons <p> Conservatives <p> Has made the criminal justice system a central policy following the London Bridge attack . It has pledged to add 10,000 more prison places using ? 2.75bn to refurbish existing prisons . Promised to bring in " tougher " sentencing for the worst offenders and to end automatic halfway release from prison for those convicted of terror-related crimes . Experts have said such measures have already been taken . Will use Brexit to cut number of foreign nationals in UK prisons . <p> Labour <p> Will restore total prison officer numbers to 2010 levels and ensure no prison staff work alone . Pledged to bring PFI prisons back under government ownership and vowed to stop creation of private prisons . Will introduce a presumption against prison sentences of six months or less for non-violent and non-sexual offences . Jeremy Corbyn said those convicted of terrorism offences should " not necessarily " serve full sentence . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Would recruit 2,000 more prison staff to help with rehabilitation of prisoners . Will introduce a presumption against short sentences and end prison terms for those possessing drugs for personal use . Promises to improve probation services and boost mental health treatment in the criminal justice system . <p> Green Party <p> Vows to halve the prison population by following policies introduced by the Netherlands and will expand restorative justice programmes to replace shorter jail terms , which the party believes have a better record of preventing reoffending . <h> Brexit Party <p> The party is light on reforms to the criminal justice system . Its political " contract with the people " says the party will introduce sentence " ranges " for young offenders to " encourage rehabilitation " . Party leader Nigel Farage said during the campaign convicted terrorists should not be released from prison . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Is opposed to the building of large-scale " super prisons " in Wales , and aims to cut the proportionally high prisoner numbers in Wales by scrapping short-term sentences , particularly for women . Will use suspended sentences for women charged with non-violent crimes and support dedicated , small , prison or secure centres for female prisoners in Wales . <h> Special relationship <p> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson has sought to ally himself with Donald Trump and will prioritise getting a trade deal with the US within three years . But the Tories are adamant they will walk away from trade negotiations rather than compromise the UK 's existing animal welfare standards or open up the NHS to privatisation by American firms . <p> Labour <p> The party is strongly opposed to what it calls " the outsourcing of UK foreign policy to US President Donald Trump " , suggesting Jeremy Corbyn would break with decades of precedent to distance the UK from America on the international stage . He has also promised to pressure Mr Trump to take more action on climate change . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The party 's manifesto says : " President Trump has repeatedly acted to cause instability , whether by initiating trade wars or abandoning Kurdish allies in Syria . " The Lib Dems would prioritise working through multilateral bodies such as the UN over the bilateral relationship between Britain and America . <p> Green Party <p> The Greens want to strengthen the UN as a forum for protecting the climate , rather than focussing on traditional state-to-state diplomacy . A number of their policies , such as declaring the whole of the Arctic a " world nature reserve " which can not be developed , would set up a clash with the US . The Greens ' strict conditions for striking trade deals would rule out any realistic transatlantic agreement . <p> Brexit Party <p> Nigel Farage is a long-standing friend of Mr Trump and is enthusiastic about the possibility of a trade deal between Britain and the US after Brexit . He has dismissed the suggestion the NHS could be damaged by any free-trade agreement . <p> SNP <p> Despite Donald Trump 's close ties to Scotland , including his business interests , SNP ministers have been quick to attack the US President over his views on immigration and human rights . The party 's manifesto also warns of a " real risk " that a post-Brexit UK-US trade deal will open up the NHS to multinational health firms and proposes a new law to stop this from happening . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Plaid supports several policies including scrapping nuclear weapons which would be opposed by the US government . The party also says : " In the event of leaving the EU , we will strongly oppose the inclusion of the Welsh NHS within any future trade deals with the USA . " <p> Ukip <p> Ukip says Britain " should not allow ourselves to be swept into war on someone else 's coattails " in a suggestion the party would resist joining the US in future military action . <p> In summary <p> Only the Tories and the Brexit Party are enthusiastic about working with the USA under the current Trump administration . Other parties say they would stand up to the President while a Labour government would usher in a totally new era in transatlantic relations . <h> China/Russia <p> Conservatives <p> Boris Johnson wants a post-Brexit trade deal with China but has not put a timeframe on it . He is keen for the country to end its trade war with the US . The Conservatives say that Russia should be held to account for " destabilising activity " in other countries , such as election manipulation and targeted assassinations , but have so far refused to release a parliamentary report into its behaviour . <p> Labour <p> Labour has demanded the instant release of the report into alleged Russian meddling in British elections . Jeremy Corbyn has denied benefiting from Russian hacking himself , after the leak of a document describing US-UK trade talks . He has said Britain should do more to hold China to account over its human-rights record . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> The UK government should support Ukraine in its struggle to shake off Russian domination , and challenge Vladimir Putin for " persistently threatening the international rules-based order " . Jo Swinson has previously praised China 's government as a " voice of reason " in international relations , but the party criticises the regime 's treatment of the Uighur people . <p> Green Party <p> The Greens want to work with China and other large developing countries to ensure their economic growth does not result in environmental destruction . It has called for tougher action on allies of Putin who are able to stash their money in the UK without being held to account for how they came by it . <p> Brexit Party <p> Sceptical of claims Russia has interfered in British elections , calling them " baseless propaganda and scare stories used to shut down debate " . Nigel Farage has demanded greater curbs on the import of cheap steel from China , claiming it has harmed the industry in the UK . <p> SNP <p> Foreign policy is reserved to Westminster , but with Chinese tourism booming in Scotland , SNP ministers have promoted the economic ties and cultural links between the two countries . On Russia , the party 's defence spokesman Stewart McDonald has been a vocal critic of Vladimir Putin , hitting out at the " heavy fist " of the Kremlin in dealing with its neighbours . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> MPs from Plaid Cymru have demanded that the UK government stand up to China on the issue of Tibet . The party cast doubt on the evidence Vladimir Putin 's government was responsible for the nerve agent attack on Salisbury last year . <p> Ukip <p> In the past senior Ukip figures have repeatedly been accused of links to Russia - but also claim to have been targeted by Russian meddling designed to suppress their vote . Some from the party have warned against a new trade deal with China . <p> In summary <p> None of the parties has set out a detailed blueprint to deal with either Russia or China , the two global superpowers with which Britain has the most complex relationship . They are united in opposition to Vladimir Putin 's behaviour but divided on whether or not it is damaging British democracy . On China , most parties support close engagement but they are wary of being bound too tightly to the country . <h> Trident and Nato <p> Conservatives <p> We will continue to exceed the NATO target of spending 2 per cent of GDP on defence and increase the budget by at least 0.5 per cent above inflation every year of the new Parliament . We will maintain our Trident nuclear deterrent , which guarantees our security . And we will adapt to new threats , investing more in cybersecurity and setting up the UK 's first Space Command . We will stand against terrorism and extremism around the world . After Brexit , we will bolster the alliances and institutions that help project our influence and keep us safe , such as the UN and the UN Security Council and NATO . <p> Labour <p> Will increase funding for UN peacekeeping operations to ? 100 million . and maintain the UK 's commitment to NATO and close relationship with Europe . Will use the country 's influence at the United Nations to support peace and security worldwide . Supports the renewal of the Trident nuclear deterrent and will actively lead multilateral efforts under our obligations to the Non-Proliferation Treaty to create a nuclear-free world <p> Liberal Democrats <p> Commit to the principle of collective self-defence as laid out in the North Atlantic Treaty and spending two per cent of GDP on defence in line with NATO recommendations.The Lib Dems do n't mention but promise to " maintain a minimum nuclear deterrent , while pursuing multilateral nuclear disarmament . <p> Green Party <p> Would cancel the Trident weapons system and nuclear-powered submarines and work to eliminate nuclear weapons worldwide . Cash saved from scrapping Trident would be used for developing non-carbon emitting technology . <p> Brexit Party <p> There is no mention of Trident . Nigel Farage 's party would ensure that the UK maintains its commitment to NATO . <p> SNP <p> Strongly against the renewal of Trident and wants the nuclear submarines to be removed permanently from Scotland , describing them as " immoral , ineffective and expensive " . Nicola Sturgeon has said this would be a " red line " in any talks with Labour after the election . The party is currently in favour of Nato membership - provided that Trident is removed from Scotland . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> Plaid Cymru has consistently opposed what it calls the hugely wasteful and dangerous replacement of Trident , which is expected to cost at least ? 205 billion . It would scrap the scheme and spend the money on public services and infrastructure . Would oppose attempts to site nuclear weapons in Wales or Welsh waters . The manifesto does n't mention Nato . <h> Overseas Aid <p> Conservatives <p> After Brexit , will bolster the alliances and institutions that help boost trade such as the Commonwealth ; the G20 ; the G7 ; and the World Trade Organisation . " We will open new markets and support free trade and global growth . " <p> Labour <p> Will end ' bomb first , talk later ' approach and instead have a foreign policy based on peace , justice and human rights . Will immediately suspend the sale of arms to Saudi Arabia for use in Yemen and to Israel for arms used in violation of the human rights of Palestinian civilians . Will conduct a root-and-branch reform of arms exports regime . <p> Liberal Democrats <p> We commit to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income on aid . This would be spent reducing poverty , defending human rights , protecting the environment and preventing violent conflict worldwide . We would also work to controlling arms exports to countries with poor human rights records and , as part of this , suspend arms sales to Saudi Arabia . Would promote democracy and stability in Ukraine and neighbouring countries against an increasingly aggressive Russia . <p> Green Party <p> Would phase in an increase in spending on foreign aid from 0.7 per cent to 1 per cent of our gross national income ( GNI ) , making us the third highest donor , by that measure , in the world by 2021 . Ensure that all UK aid is aimed at the poorest , and is locally designed , appropriate and subject to local scrutiny . Where feasible , aid will be given as grants , not loans . <p> Brexit Party <p> The party would cut the foreign aid budget in half , saving ? 40bn over the five-year term and spend the money to boost UK services instead . Pledges to stop the tragedy associated with human trafficking . <p> Plaid Cymru <p> The party wants Wales to be a nation of sanctuary for refugees fleeing war and oppression and will help refugees and asylum seekers integrate into Welsh society . Future trade deals taken by the UK , whether inside or outside the EU , should maintain and enhance environmental standards , minimise the environmental footprint of trade and make trade terms explicitly subject to environmental and human rights commitments .

@@41553848 <h> Election manifestos -- bona fide or bluster ? <h> A lot of resources are put into drafting and launching an election manifesto but Political Correspondent John Manley wonders how much attention voters pay to them and to what degree parties stay true to their pledges <p> IT 'S fair to assume that only the most politically nerdy among you have read one -- never mind all -- of the manifestos published by Northern Ireland 's main parties ahead of Thursday 's Westminster poll . <p> They tend not to be widely distributed and even those who receive a physical copy are likely to discard them relatively quickly , rarely returning to their contents to see if a party has remained true to its pledges . <p> However , if you are especially keen to scrutinise a party 's policy proposals , the documents are available on their respective websites . <p> The manifesto serves two primary purposes . <p> It sets out a party 's stall , showcasing the policy areas they regard as important and how in the event of assuming power they would address these issues . Canvassers should ideally have studied the manifesto 's contents and be well equipped to answer questions from inquisitive constituents . <p> A manifesto 's other main purpose is to provide a focus for the media at its launch , ensuring a party receives coverage of its campaign , candidates and key policy initiatives . <p> This is n't always necessarily positive , as the DUP will testify , having had to endure a degree of ridicule after advocating firstly a bridge to Scotland and more recently , interconnection with Iceland , enabling households and businesses in Northern Ireland to utilise power generated by the island 's volcanoes . <p> But to give the Arlene Foster 's party its due , its manifestos tend to be better researched and presented than the rest . <p> Alan Meban of the Slugger O'Toole website points to the limited influence of the north 's 18 representatives in a parliament of 650 MPs and says the likelihood of any party 's policies being adopted to a notable degree is remote . <p> " Most Westminster manifestos are aspirational stuff because there 's very little prospect of Northern Ireland parties wielding the necessary power to implement their pledges , " he says . <p> He also notes how the north 's parties tend to fill their general election manifestos with devolved issues that do n't fall under Westminster 's remit . <p> " There 's lots of local issues in each of the manifestos despite the fact that those elected tend not to have responsibility at that level , " he says . <p> On the manifestos published in recent weeks , he describes Alliance 's as " wordy and quite detailed " , the SDLP 's is " careful not to have too many pledges , with a strong focus on Brexit " , while the Ulster Unionists provide an inadvertent reminder that only one of its 16 candidates is female . <p> " Sinn F ? in 's manifesto is all about Brexit and unity but in the meantime the health crisis has become the major issue of the election , and their manifesto is quite weak in that regard , " says Mr Meban . <p> " The DUP has quite a lot of detail on a lot of issues , reflecting the party 's potential to be in a position of power similar after the 2017 election when they struck the confidence and supply deal with the Tories . <p> " If there 's a hung parliament they can simply hand over the document to whoever they 're dealing with and say ' these are the sort of issues that concern us ' . " <p> He points out that few parties ever spell out the detail of their pledges and few are ever held to account on the content of their previous manifestos . <p> Ulster University senior economist Esmond Birnie highlights how the north 's five parties make a lot of spending commitments but almost none are costed . <p> Similarly , they tend to promise tax cuts yet it is " extremely rare " for them to advocate a reduction in public spending . <p> He says that all the main parties have " come up with some genuinely good ideas " . <p> " But sometimes their plans could be described as too clever by half -- sophisticated but not likely to survive contact with various realities , including HM Treasury . " <p> Overall , the material in the manifestos tends to veer towards vague , broad brush ambitions rather than carefully costed , detailed policy that could be adopted within weeks of the election . <p> Arguably nothing illustrates this better than the pledges to combat climate change , a policy area that has tended to be overlooked by Northern Ireland 's parties in the past but has suddenly become fashionable , even with those parties whose ranks include people who deny man-made climate change . <p> The manifestos are replete with soundbites about " climate catastrophe " , " zero-carbon targets " and a " clean , green future " , yet none outlines how to address specifically emissions from the north 's agriculture sector , the single biggest contributor to the region 's climate change gas output . <p> : : : : : : : : : : : : : <p> BITE-SIZE MANIFESTOS <p> Alliance -- Oppose Brexit and advocate a second referendum ; reduce the UK 's net greenhouse emissions ; make political donations more transparent . 
@@41554104 <p> Professor Bert Bolin was a multi-award-winning Swedish meteorologist who spent much of his life as a pioneering scientific statesman and was instrumental in developing and promoting climate research . Bolin worked tirelessly on the subject during the Sixties and Seventies . Then in 1987 he contributed substantially to the 500-page Brundtland Report that served as a warning to the world of the rise in global temperatures and helped persuade the United Nations to create the Intergovernmental Panel On Climate Change . You probably have n't heard of him . <p> You know Greta Thunberg , though . The 16-year-old Swedish activist has significantly raised worldwide awareness of the climate crisis , met with ( and chastised ) world leaders and appeared on the cover of Time magazine , which described her as a " next-generation leader " . Thanks to Thunberg , millions of young people and adults from 150 countries have taken part in Global Climate Strikes . And she has achieved all that in the space of just over a year . <p> Inspired by their fellow Swedes , Gothenberg-based Volvo has committed to doing its bit . From next year , the carmaker 's target is that no one should be killed or seriously injured in a new Volvo and intends to reduce the top speed of all its cars to 112mph . Volvo is also the first major premium car company to commit to having only hybrid or fully electric powertrains for all its vehicles and by 2025 plans to use recycled material to produce at least 25 per cent of its in-car plastics and for its global manufacturing operations to be carbon neutral . All of which are fine sentiments , but they would n't mean much if Volvo did not have a track record of acting responsibly and making cars that people actually want to drive . Fortunately , Volvo does . Like Bolin , Volvo also quietly spent decades working on what it believed in , such as developing safety systems including the first three-point seatbelt ( 1959 ) , rear-facing child seats ( 1972 ) , side-impact protection ( 1991 ) and a blind spot information system ( 2004 ) -- all of which would become industry standard on most new cars . Like Thunberg , Volvo has challenged the public 's perception and convinced people to take notice . <p> Volvo is the first major car company to commit to having only hybrid or fully electric powertrains <p> And the XC40 is the model that has taken the brand to the next level . Named European Car Of The Year in 2018 , it is a compact SUV that manages to be both clever and the epitome of Scandi cool . For a start , it looks great . Not Ferrari great , of course , but practical , muscular and sleekly understated without being generic . Its two-tone styling works well ( especially if you plump for the exterior styling kit ) , as do the 20in double-spoke wheels . It is as handsome as the daddy of off-road daddies , the Range Rover Evoque . Inside , it is even better . It feels far bigger and more refined than any compact car should and the large Sensus infotainment screen that pretty much runs the car ( Buttons ? Switches ? Do n't be a knob ) is intuitive and complemented by Apple CarPlay and a Harman Kardon surround-sound system . <p> Then there is all the stuff you ca n't see but would n't want to be without : pilot assist , city safety , run-off road protection , oncoming lane mitigation , cross-traffic alert ( with brake support ) and a 360-degree camera . What does all this stuff do ? Keeps you safe , overrides your driving errors and makes parking an absolute doddle . <p> It is n't perfect , of course . The driving experience is reliable not radical and the 34mpg figure is optimistic to say the least . Most Volvo drivers care about this stuff -- they will be delighted with the former ( and they 're right you do n't need supercar handling on the way to the recycling centre ) , but less impressed with the latter . But do n't worry : a fully electric XC40 will be here next year . When you go to buy one ( and you should ) , tell them Greta sent you ...

@@41556108 <h> Den Of Geek 's top books of 2019 <h> We asked our writers to recommend their favourite new books published this year , and here 's what they chose ... <p> Forget the vanity of the rhombus . Say no thank you to the grandiosity of triangles , cylinders and pyramids . Walk away from too-too spheres and cubes , and thrust forward the flat palm of no to the brazenly non-geometrical . The only shape gift you want to receive at this time of year is the rectangle . The true shape . The shape of a book . <h> This Is How You Lose the Time War by Max Gladstone and Amal El-Mohtar <p> A technocratic cyber timeline is warring against an outer space biopunk Garden of Eden timeline up and down history . Then , on one particularly bloody battlefield , a soldier on one side of the war leaves a letter to the other . The exchange of letters that follows makes for a quick read , but with language you 'll want to linger over . It 's a small , intimate story about only two characters , but against the most epic backdrop you could ask for . In this war Atlantis falls over and over again , vast temples of bone exist in long forgotten pre-history , and futuristic scavengers build religions around Siri . But it is all just that , backdrop to the story of these two characters , scenery that the book dashes past without look back . It cares less about world building than it does about the imagery it provides for a wild and surprising love story . <p> Chris Farnell <h> My Sister The Serial Killer by Oyinkan Braithwaite <p> This black comedy treads the line between funny and unsettling really well . There 's a lot going on here based on the sisters ' relationship , appearance and reaction to violent death . Combining elements of satire , crime and horror it 's a well-paced book that combines the ratcheting tension of murder with banalities of work and family life . The plot gets satisfying thicker and the characterization is thorough all the way through to the supporting characters . <p> I can imagine fans ofInside Number 9 finding a lot to enjoy from this one . It feels tonally similar to something that show would try as well as featuring a flawed central double act . <p> Andrew Blair <h> The Blue Salt Road by Joanne Harris <p> Flora the gunnerman 's daughter is beautiful , proud and cruel . Offering a fascinating , fraught and often very funny look at the life and times of the 1980s heyday of comedy in Hollywood , de Semlyen leaves no stone unturned in telling the story of the impulsive and eccentric stars behind countless classics of the time . A hazy , drug-fuelled era of egos and excess , the book captures the vivid ups and downs of life in the hallowed halls of Saturday Night Live and National Lampoon 's as well as offering insights on the making of everything from Ghostbusters to Beverly Hills Cop thanks to a glut of great interviews and meticulously researched behind-the-scenes details . <p> Jack Beresford <h> Little Weirds by Jenny Slate <p> This is not your typical book written by a celebrity . Instead of funny anecdotes from childhood and tales about ' making it big ' in Hollywood , Jenny Slate 's ( most well-known for her role as Mona-Lisa Saperstein on Parks And Recreation ) Little Weirds is a series of unique personal essays on love , womanhood , intimacy and much more . Written after what she calls " pummelling heartbreak " , Slate takes us inside her mind with astounding vulnerability and creativity . From comparing herself to a Parisian croissant to wistfully reimagining her divorce , she never flinches away from the goriness of it all ; the loneliness and the pain , especially , are conveyed so vividly , they feel almost too raw for strangers like us to experience . It provides a fascinating counterpoint to many of the perceived ideas espoused by the earlier books , questioning the value of rational thinking if it strips life of its colour and mysteries . Pullman imbues this new volume with a peculiar spirituality that enriches , rather than contradicts , the atheist sensibilities of the original trilogy . Unquestionably not for children , The Secret Commonwealth offers a bittersweet answer to the question of what happened to Lyra Silvertongue , proving that Pullman 's epic saga has grown up along with his audience . Imperfect but essential . <p> Gabriel Bergmoser <h> Making Moon -- A British Sci-Fi Cult Classic by Nathan Parker <p> Earlier this year , a live orchestra performed Clint Mansell 's atmospheric score to a screening of Duncan Jones ' debut feature Moon at London 's Barbican Centre . Harris <p> In a bid to save her failing marriage , Kate Keeling moves to Haverscroft House , only to find that there is more going on in the house than meets the eye . S.A. Harris delivers a wonderfully spooky story that really delivers on both atmosphere and tension . Henry takes us right back to his childhood in Dudley , growing up in challenging circumstances , one hand with a strict but loving mother pushing the entire family to intergrate into British society and on the other a society that was n't willing or able to accept anybody different into their communities . Henry weaves hilarious family stories in with truly heartbreaking accounts of the torrent of racism he had to encounter on his journey to one of the UK 's most beloved entertainers . One such being a soul-destroying account of a childhood friendship of toy sharing and daily playdates which were severed in a letterbox altercation which would break even the coldest of hearts . <p> However , in true Henry style , there is never a moment to wallow or become bitter as he makes his way up the comedy ranks , playing unfriendly comedy clubs ( and turning the room into his favour ) , winning New Faces and becoming part of the TV establishment . <p> There is time for reflection and even questioning of certain career choices ( it is a fasninating read to see him pick apart his role in the Minstral Show for example ) and of his early life , with the inclusion of beautiful graphic novel pains that tell the story of Henry finding out who his biological father was . <p> Ultimately Henry 's story ( and this is only part of it - two more books are to follow to cover the 80s and beyond ) is hugely inspirational and is a living breathing picture of growing up as a Black British child in the 60s and 70s , finding fame and starting a journey which would lead to him becoming a Knight of the Realm . <p> You wo n't read anything as honest , heartbreaking or funny this year . <p> Carley Tauchert-Hutchins <h> The Testaments by Margaret Atwood <p> Arguably this year 's biggest literary event and the joint-winner of the 2019 Booker prize ( alongside Bernadine Evaristo for Girl , Woman , Other ) , Margaret Atwood 's sequel to 1985 's The Handmaid 's Tale hardly needs any more publicity , but it 's getting some here because it deserves the praise . Enter the dystopian future driven by a satanic President Razour , and an army of A.I. soldiers and BattlemaGes* at his command . Omnipotent government is everywhere , plugged into peoples ' thoughts and emotions through cyber tech . And mankind is plummeting towards hell . Literally . Sharp , wry and funny , with a dose of theology for good measure , Adcock imbues his dystopian future with wit , drawing numerous narrative threads together with skill , and a host of explanatory footnotes and acronyms that on occasion boggled my not particularly scientific mind . Jump aboard L2 , embrace the darkness and enjoy the ride . <p> Jane Roberts-Morpeth <h> Water Shall Refuse Them by Lucie McKnight-Hardie <p> It 's the sweltering summer of 1976 and sixteen year old Nif is forced to move to a tiny Welsh village as her family attempts to come to terms with the accidental drowning of her sister . Nif practices her own brand of witchcraft and when a local teen takes an interest in her , sinister events begin to unfurl . Water Shall Refuse Them delights in its folk horror leanings as well as using the Welsh landscape to stunning effect . Lucie McKnight Hardy 's debut is reminiscent of Shirley Jackson in its calm narration and Nif is a character who lingers long in the memory . <p> Becky Lea <h> Strange Planet : The Comic Sensation Of The Year by Nathan Pyle <p> If the words " I crave star damage " pass through your mind whenever you see a tanned torso on an exotic beach holiday tube ad , then you 've already met the work of New York cartoonist Nathan Pyle . A hit webcomic artist ( he 's **25;28;TOOLONG on Instagram ) , his single to four-panel cartoons featuring alien-ish humanoid creatures narrating banal life experiences highlight the absurdity of social convention and human tradition . The odd one-bounce of a handshake , the giving of dead flowers on Valentine 's Day , the not-remotely-fresh drinking of vintage wine ... his skewed take on the day-to-day is funny , warm , instantly relatable and once seen , pretty much unforgettable . This book , collecting the Strange Planet panels , makes a lovely gift . <p> Louisa Mellor <h> A Good Girl 's Guide To Murder by Holly Jackson <p> It should come as no surprise that the author of this compelling YA mystery is a true-crime nut . The twist : the girl was killed five years ago and her assailant was arrested by police . But what if the police got it wrong ? Cleverly unravelling her mystery via journal entries , interview transcripts , maps and more , Jackson weaves a gripping yarn that never goes where you expect and feels chillingly authentic . The really good news ? Sequel Good Girl , Bad Blood is out in April 2020 . The fantasy that James creates is infused with African folklore and provides an exciting new world for a familiar genre plot . It 's an initially tricky book to get into , but when it clicks into gear , James ' fantasy is an exciting , hallucinatory trip across a dangerous and wild landscape . The second and third instalments of the trilogy will explore the same events as Black Leopard Red Wolf in a Rashomon style story of shifting perspectives and uncertain truths . <p> Becky Lea <h> The Migration by Helen Marshall <p> Floods , storms , landscapes swept away : but in The Migration it 's not only terrain that is altered by climate change . And there are rumours that their corpses are starting to change too . <p> You could label this as a fresh take on zombies , or climate fiction , but really it 's a creation all of its own , mixing different and surprising elements for a confronting - but far from hopeless - look at humanity 's future .
